teile.einleitung: World Heritage means places all over the world that are so unique and valuable that they should be protected for the whole of humanity. UNESCO, an organisation of the United Nations, keeps a list of cultural monuments and natural landscapes for this. Switzerland, too, has many World Heritage Sites, from the old town of Bern to the Aletsch Glacier.
wichtigste: UNESCO names especially valuable places as World Heritage.
The basis is the World Heritage Convention of 1972.
There is cultural heritage, natural heritage and mixed sites.
The list contains more than 1,000 sites in more than 160 countries.
The old town of Bern, the Abbey of St Gall and the Convent of Müstair have been World Heritage since 1983.
Well-known World Heritage Sites are the Taj Mahal in India and Machu Picchu in Peru.
Countries with World Heritage commit themselves to protecting and looking after these places.

abschnitte.text: **UNESCO** is the United Nations organisation for education, science and culture. In 1972 many countries agreed the **World Heritage Convention**. In it they promise to protect extraordinary places together. Every year a committee decides which new sites are added to the list. In 2025 the list contained about 1,250 sites.

**Cultural heritage** includes buildings, old towns, ruins and cultural landscapes made by people. **Natural heritage** includes mountain ranges, forests, reefs or places with important fossils. Some sites are both at once. If a World Heritage Site is threatened, for example by war, natural disasters or too much building, it is put on the **List of World Heritage in Danger**.

The **old town of Bern**, with its long arcades, has been World Heritage since 1983. In the same year the **Abbey of St Gall**, with its Baroque abbey library, and the Convent of St John in **Müstair** in the Grisons were added. The three castles of **Bellinzona** in Ticino used to protect the town and the valley. The vineyard terraces of **Lavaux** on Lake Geneva and the watchmaking towns of La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle also belong to it. The Albula and Bernina lines of the Rhaetian Railway are World Heritage too.

The **Jungfrau-Aletsch** region, with the largest glacier in the Alps, became World Heritage in 2001. At **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, many fossils of sea creatures and reptiles from the Triassic period have been found. The Tectonic Arena Sardona shows how older rocks were pushed over younger ones when the Alps formed. In all, Switzerland has 13 World Heritage Sites (as of 2025).

The **Taj Mahal** in India is a magnificent tomb of white marble. The ruler Shah Jahan had it built in the 17th century for his late wife. **Machu Picchu** is an Inca city high in the Andes of Peru. Other well-known sites are the Great Wall of China, the Pyramids of Giza and the Great Barrier Reef in Australia.

begriffe.erklaerung: The United Nations organisation for education, science and culture.
A treaty that many countries sign together.
A landscape shaped by people’s work, for example vineyards.
A covered walkway along houses, under which you can walk and stay dry.

gewusst: The Abbey Library of St Gall has manuscripts that are more than 1,000 years old.
A place can also be taken off the World Heritage List again if it is not well protected.
Machu Picchu only became widely known to the public in 1911.

teile.einleitung: Sustainable materials are kind to the environment when they are made, used and disposed of. They should need as little energy, water and harmful substances as possible. They include new ideas for cycles, but also old plant fibres such as hemp.
wichtigste: **Cradle to Cradle** means that all materials should stay in cycles.
In **upcycling** something more valuable is made from waste, in **downcycling** something of lower value.
**Lyocell** is made from wood cellulose in a closed solvent cycle.
A **life cycle assessment** looks at the environmental effects over the whole life of a product.
The textile standard **bluesign** was founded in Switzerland in 2000.
**Hemp** grows quickly and hardly needs any pesticides.

abschnitte.text: The chemist **Michael Braungart** and the architect **William McDonough** developed the concept of **Cradle to Cradle**. The idea is that products should be designed so that there is no more waste. Materials are either **biodegradable** and return to nature. Or they are completely recycled as technical raw materials.

In **upcycling**, something more valuable is made from waste. A well-known example comes from Zurich: since the 1990s the company **Freitag** has been sewing bags from old lorry tarpaulins. In **downcycling**, on the other hand, the material loses quality. This happens, for example, when waste paper is turned into cardboard. Both are better than throwing things away, but upcycling keeps the value better.

**Lyocell** is a fibre made from the cellulose in wood. The cellulose is dissolved in a solvent that is almost completely recovered. The fibre is soft and biodegradable. **Hemp** grows quickly, needs little crop protection and keeps weeds down by itself. Its tear-resistant fibres are suitable for fabrics, ropes and **insulation mats** for houses.

A **life cycle assessment** shows whether a material is really environmentally friendly. It covers the whole life of a product: obtaining raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal. This makes it possible to compare different materials fairly. Sometimes it turns out that a natural material does worse than expected because of long transport routes.

Many **chemicals** are often used in making clothes, for example for dyeing. The **bluesign** system was founded in Switzerland in 2000. It checks whether companies avoid substances that harm the environment and health during production. Many makers of outdoor and sports clothing work with this standard.

gewusst: A piece of a used lorry tarpaulin is used for each Freitag bag, which is why every bag is one of a kind.
Hemp is one of the oldest fibre plants that people grow.

teile.einleitung: Nam June Paik was an artist who came from Korea and worked in Germany and the USA. He is seen as the pioneer and “father” of video art. With television sets he created works of art that were completely new at the time.
wichtigste: Nam June Paik was born in Seoul in 1932 and died in 2006.
He is seen as the pioneer and “father” of **video art**.
From the 1960s he worked with altered television sets.
He belonged to the artists’ group **Fluxus**.
He lived and worked in Germany and in New York, among other places.
His work “TV Buddha” is well known.

abschnitte.text: Nam June Paik was born **in Seoul in 1932**. He first studied music, among other places in Japan and Germany. In Germany he got to know the composer **John Cage**, who experimented with noises and chance. This had a strong influence on Paik. He became part of the **Fluxus** movement, in which artists played with actions and everyday things.

In 1963 Paik showed an exhibition in Wuppertal with several **television sets**. He had altered them so that the pictures appeared distorted and warped. That was something completely new at the time. Television was a medium for news and entertainment, not for art. Paik showed that you can also work artistically with electronic images.

One of his best-known works is **“TV Buddha”**. A Buddha figure sits in front of a television. A camera films it, and the television shows exactly this picture. So the Buddha looks at itself in an endless loop. The work makes you think about television, time and looking at yourself.

From the mid-1960s Paik lived mainly in **New York**. But he was also a professor at the art academy in **Düsseldorf**. Later he built large installations from dozens of screens. Many **media artists** still see him as a model today. His works are in museums all over the world.

gewusst: Paik was one of the first artists to work with a portable video camera.
In South Korea there is an art centre named after Nam June Paik.

teile.einleitung: An electric circuit is the path along which electric current flows. Only when this path is closed does a lamp light up or a motor turn. In handicraft lessons you build simple circuits with batteries.
wichtigste: Current only flows in a closed circuit.
A simple circuit has a battery, wires and a lamp.
A switch opens and closes the circuit.
Metals conduct electricity, plastic and wood do not.
You must never experiment with electricity from the socket.

abschnitte.text: A simple circuit consists of a **power source**, for example a battery, **wires** and a **device** that uses the electricity, such as a lamp. The battery has two terminals, a **positive terminal** and a **negative terminal**. Current only flows if there is an unbroken path from one terminal through the lamp to the other terminal. Any break stops the current immediately, and the lamp goes out.

A **switch** opens or closes the circuit. When it is switched on, two metal parts touch and the current can flow. When it is switched off, a gap appears. The light switch at home works like this too. You can build a simple switch yourself, for example from a paper clip and two drawing pins.

Materials that conduct electricity well are called **conductors**. They include metals such as copper, iron or aluminium. That is why cables have copper wire inside. Materials such as plastic, rubber, glass or dry wood hardly conduct electricity. They are called **insulators**. They cover the cables so that you can touch them safely.

For experiments you only use **batteries** with a low voltage. The electricity from the **socket** in Switzerland has 230 volts and can kill. You must never experiment with it. If you connect the two terminals of a battery directly with a wire, you get a **short circuit**. The wire gets hot and the battery quickly goes flat.

gewusst: If you connect several lamps one after another in a circuit, they all go out if one breaks. This is called a series circuit.
The human body also conducts electricity, which is why electricity from the socket is so dangerous.

teile.einleitung: A non-fungible token, NFT for short, is a digital record that marks a particular object as unique. It is stored on a blockchain. In 2021 NFTs of digital works of art became known all over the world.
wichtigste: NFT stands for “non-fungible token”, a token that cannot be exchanged one for one.
An NFT is stored on a **blockchain**, often on Ethereum.
An NFT shows who owns a particular digital record.
Buying an NFT does not automatically give you the copyright.
In 2021 the work “Everydays: The First 5000 Days” by Beeple was auctioned for about 69 million US dollars.
After the great rush in 2021, many prices fell sharply.

abschnitte.text: A franc is fungible, that is, exchangeable: every franc is worth the same as any other. An **NFT**, on the other hand, is **non-fungible**. Every NFT is unique and has its own identifier. It works like a digital certificate of authenticity. It can belong, for example, to a picture, a video or an item in a game.

NFTs are stored on a **blockchain**. This is a kind of digital ledger that is kept on a great many computers at the same time. Entries in it can hardly be forged or deleted. Many NFTs use the **Ethereum** blockchain. The blockchain records who owns an NFT and who it was sold to.

In March 2021 the famous auction house **Christie’s** auctioned a digital work by the artist **Beeple**. It is called “Everydays: The First 5000 Days”. The work is a collage of 5,000 pictures that Beeple had created on consecutive days. It was sold as an NFT for around **69 million US dollars**. As a result, digital art suddenly became a talking point all over the world.

Supporters say that digital artists can sell their works directly with NFTs. Critics point out that an NFT is only a record: anyone can still copy the picture itself. The **copyright** also usually stays with the artist. Ethereum used to need a great deal of electricity, but since 2022 much less. After 2021 the prices of many NFTs fell sharply, and interest died down.

gewusst: Before Beeple’s work was auctioned, he had made a new digital picture every day for more than 13 years.
So many blockchain companies have settled in the canton of Zug that the region is called “Crypto Valley”.

teile.einleitung: Music is written on a **staff** (also called a stave). It consists of five horizontal lines, which are also called a line of music. The higher a note sits on it, the higher the note sounds.
wichtigste: The staff has five lines and four spaces.
The bottom line is the first line.
Notes sit on the lines or in the spaces.
The clef is at the beginning of the line of music.
For low notes the bass clef is used.
Short lines above or below the staff are called ledger lines.
The double line at the end of a piece is called the final barline.

abschnitte.text: The staff consists of **five lines**. Between them are **four spaces**. You count from the bottom to the top: the **bottom line** is the first, the top line the fifth. A note can sit **on a line**, and then the line goes right through the middle of the note head. Or it sits **in a space** between two lines.

Right at the **beginning of the line of music** is the **clef**. It shows which notes are on which lines. The **treble clef** is for high notes, for example for the violin, the flute or the right hand on the piano. The **bass clef** is for low notes, for example for the cello or the left hand.

Some notes are too high or too low for the five lines. Then you draw short extra lines above or below, the **ledger lines**. In the treble clef the first ledger line below the five lines carries **C**, more precisely c¹ (middle C). On the piano this note lies roughly in the middle.

Vertical lines divide the music into **bars**; they are called **barlines**. At the very end of a piece there is a **final barline**: a thin and a thick line next to each other. If there are also two dots in front of it, it is a **repeat sign**, and then you play a section again.

In the past melodies were written down only with signs above the words. Around the year 1000 the monk **Guido of Arezzo** in Italy suggested using lines. That way the pitch could be read exactly. Over time our modern staff with five lines developed from this.

gewusst: For the piano two staves are joined with a curly bracket (a brace), one for each hand.
A conductor's score can have more than twenty staves one below the other, one for each part.

teile.einleitung: “Spiral Jetty” is a famous work of art by the American artist Robert Smithson. It is a huge spiral of stones in the Great Salt Lake in Utah, USA.
wichtigste: Robert Smithson created “Spiral Jetty” in 1970.
The work is in the Great Salt Lake in the US state of Utah.
The spiral is around 460 metres long.
It is made of basalt rock and earth.
Depending on the water level, it is visible or under water.
The work is seen as a major work of land art.

abschnitte.text: In 1970 **Robert Smithson** had basalt rock and earth tipped into the **Great Salt Lake**. For this he used lorries and building machines. This created a spiral that leads from the shore far out into the water. It is around **460 metres** long. You can see its shape best from above.

“Spiral Jetty” belongs to **land art**. In this art movement, artists work directly in the landscape and with materials from nature. The works are not in a museum, but outdoors. Wind, water and weather change them over time. That is deliberately part of the work of art.

The water level of the Great Salt Lake varies a great deal. Shortly after it was built, the water rose and the spiral disappeared beneath the surface for many years. Later the lake sank and it reappeared, now covered with white **salt crusts**. The water in this part of the lake often has a reddish shimmer, because tiny living things that can stand a lot of salt live in it.

gewusst: Smithson also made a film about the spiral, in which you can see it from a helicopter.

teile.einleitung: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, draughtsman and sculptor and is seen as one of the most important artists of the 20th century. Together with a friend he invented Cubism, in which faces and things are put together from angular shapes. His pictures often look quite different from what you expect, and that is exactly what makes them so exciting.
wichtigste: Pablo Picasso was born in Málaga in Spain in 1881.
His father was a painter and art teacher and encouraged him from childhood.
In his “Blue Period”, Picasso painted almost all his pictures in shades of blue.
Together with Georges Braque he founded Cubism.
His large picture “Guernica” condemns the horrors of war.
A dove that he drew became a worldwide symbol of peace.
Picasso also made sculptures, ceramics and pots.
He died in France in 1973 at the age of 91.

abschnitte.text: Picasso was born on 25 October 1881 in **Málaga** in southern Spain. His father José Ruiz Blasco was a painter and art teacher. Even as a teenager Pablo drew as well as an adult. He studied at art schools in Barcelona and Madrid. From 1904 he lived almost always in **France**, at first in Paris.

From about 1901 to 1904 Picasso painted almost only in shades of blue, which is why it is called the **Blue Period**. The pictures often show poor, sad or lonely people. This was followed by the **Rose Period**, with warmer colours. These pictures often show travelling entertainers, acrobats and harlequins.

In 1907 Picasso painted the picture “Les Demoiselles d’Avignon”, which shocked many people at the time. Together with the Frenchman **Georges Braque** he then developed **Cubism**. In it, people and objects are broken down into angular areas. Sometimes you see a face from the front and from the side at the same time. Later the two also glued pieces of paper into their pictures, an early form of collage.

abschnitte.titel: Guernica and the dove of peace
abschnitte.text: In the Spanish Civil War, the Basque town of Guernica was bombed from the air in 1937. In response Picasso painted the huge black, white and grey picture **“Guernica”**, which is almost eight metres wide. It shows screaming people and animals and is seen as one of the best-known anti-war pictures. Today it hangs in the Reina Sofía Museum in Madrid. In 1949 a lithograph by Picasso showing a **dove** became the poster of a peace congress and so a symbol of peace.

Picasso was not only a painter, but also a sculptor. He built figures from metal, wood and even from found objects such as a bicycle seat and handlebars. From the 1940s he worked with potters in **Vallauris** in the south of France. There he painted and shaped thousands of plates, jugs and vases in **ceramics**.

Picasso worked into old age and created tens of thousands of works in all. He died on 8 April 1973 in Mougins in France. There are museums with his works, for example, in Barcelona, Paris and Málaga. In Switzerland, the people of **Basel** voted in 1967 to buy two Picasso pictures for the Kunstmuseum. Picasso was so pleased that he gave the city more works.

begriffe.erklaerung: An art style in which things are broken down into angular shapes and areas.
A stage in an artist’s life in which their works look similar.
Objects made of clay that are fired in a kiln and become hard.
A print made by a process that lets you reproduce a picture on paper.

gewusst: Picasso’s full baptismal name consists of more than ten first names.
His daughter Paloma was named after the Spanish word for dove.
Picasso created more works than almost any other artist, including paintings, drawings, prints and ceramics.

teile.einleitung: Symbolism is a movement in art and literature at the end of the 19th century, from about 1880 to 1910. The artists did not simply want to show what the world looks like, but to hint at feelings, ideas and states of mind through symbols. Their pictures often seem mysterious, dreamlike or solemn.
wichtigste: Symbolism began around 1880 in France and spread all over Europe.
In 1886 the poet Jean Moréas published the “Symbolist Manifesto” in “Le Figaro”.
Symbolists wanted to hint at ideas and feelings through symbols instead of copying nature exactly.
Important Swiss Symbolists are Arnold Böcklin, Ferdinand Hodler and Giovanni Segantini.
Böcklin’s “Isle of the Dead” exists in several versions.
Gustav Klimt and Edvard Munch are also counted among the Symbolists.
Symbolism paved the way for later styles such as Expressionism.

abschnitte.text: A **symbol** is a sign that stands for something else, for example a dove for peace. The Symbolists turned against **Naturalism**, which wanted to show reality as exactly as possible. They painted dreams, myths, death, love and longing. Their pictures are not meant to explain everything, but to make the viewer think and feel.

It began with poetry. Charles Baudelaire, with his collection of poems “The Flowers of Evil” from 1857, is seen as a forerunner. In 1886 **Jean Moréas** published the **“Symbolist Manifesto”** in the Paris newspaper “Le Figaro”. Other important poets were Paul Verlaine, Arthur Rimbaud and Stéphane Mallarmé.

The Frenchman **Gustave Moreau** painted splendid pictures from myths and the Bible, for example “L’Apparition”, in which the head of John the Baptist appears to Salome. Odilon Redon drew mysterious creatures and dream pictures. Young painters around Paul Sérusier and Maurice Denis called themselves the **Nabis**, after the Hebrew word for “prophets”. They painted with flat, glowing areas of colour.

From 1880, **Arnold Böcklin** from Basel painted “Isle of the Dead”, a gloomy island with cypress trees towards which a boat is travelling. One version hangs in the Kunstmuseum Basel. **Ferdinand Hodler** from Bern developed **Parallelism**, in which similar shapes and figures are repeated, for example in his picture “Night” from 1889/90. **Giovanni Segantini**, born in Arco, painted the “Alpine Triptych” in the Alps of the Grisons, with the parts “Life, Nature, Death”. It can be seen in the Segantini Museum in St Moritz.

In 1893 the Norwegian **Edvard Munch** painted “The Scream”, a picture full of fear. He is seen as a pioneer of **Expressionism**. Around 1908/09 the Viennese painter **Gustav Klimt** created the shimmering gold painting “The Kiss”. It now hangs in the Belvedere in Vienna and is one of the best-known pictures in Austria.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign or picture that stands for an idea or a feeling.
An art movement that wants to show reality as exactly as possible.
Hodler’s idea of repeating the same shapes and figures several times side by side.
A work of art made of three pictures that belong together.

gewusst: Arnold Böcklin did not name the picture “Isle of the Dead” himself; an art dealer did.
Giovanni Segantini died in 1899 on the Schafberg above Pontresina while working on the Alpine Triptych.
Klimt used real gold leaf for some of his pictures.

teile.einleitung: “Neue Grafik” was a design magazine that was published in Zurich from 1958 to 1965. It spread the ideas of Swiss graphic design all over the world. Typical features are clear grids, sans serif typefaces and a lot of order.
wichtigste: The magazine “Neue Grafik” was published in Zurich from 1958 to 1965.
Its editors were Josef Müller-Brockmann, Richard Paul Lohse, Hans Neuburg and Carlo Vivarelli.
It was in three languages: German, English and French.
It was itself strictly designed on a **grid**.
It made the **Swiss Style** of graphic design known internationally.

abschnitte.text: In 1958 four Zurich designers founded the magazine **“Neue Grafik”** (New Graphic Design): Josef Müller-Brockmann, Richard Paul Lohse, Hans Neuburg and Carlo Vivarelli. It was published until 1965. The texts were printed side by side in **three languages**: German, English and French. This meant designers in many countries could read it. The magazine presented posters, books and exhibitions.

Typical of Swiss graphic design at this time is the **design grid**. This is an invisible network of lines along which texts and pictures are lined up. It makes a page look calm and clear. “Neue Grafik” was itself strictly designed on a grid like this. It used clear **sans serif typefaces** without decorations on the letters.

This kind of design became known as the **Swiss Style** or International Typographic Style. It was meant to be objective, clear and easy to read. Companies, airports and authorities in many countries took over these ideas. The typeface **Helvetica** was also created in Switzerland at the same time. To this day the Swiss Style shapes posters, logos and websites.

gewusst: Josef Müller-Brockmann became famous especially for concert posters for the Tonhalle Zürich.
Old issues of “Neue Grafik” are sought-after collector’s items among designers today.

teile.einleitung: The clamp is a simple clamping tool for the woodwork shop and the craft corner. You use it to press parts together or hold them down on the table.
wichtigste: A clamp presses two parts firmly together.
It consists of a bar, a fixed arm and a movable arm.
The pressure is created with a spindle and a handle.
When gluing, the clamp keeps up the pressure until the glue has set.
Scraps of wood between the clamp and the workpiece prevent pressure marks.

abschnitte.text: A clamp has a long **bar** with a fixed arm at the end. A second arm can be slid along the bar. In this movable arm there is a **spindle** with a handle. You slide the arm up to the workpiece and then turn the handle tight. Because of its shape, the most common type is also called an **F-clamp**.

Wood glue holds best when the parts are pressed firmly together. The clamp keeps up this pressure until the glue has **set**, that is, become firm. Depending on the glue, this takes from a few minutes to several hours. For large surfaces you put several clamps at equal distances. If a little glue oozes out, that is a good sign that there is enough pressure.

Between the clamp and the workpiece you put small **pads** made of scrap wood. This spreads the pressure, and no marks are left. You only tighten the clamp by hand. As well as the F-clamp, there are **one-handed clamps**, which you close with a lever, and long clamps for table tops. When sawing, a clamp holds the wood safely on the workbench.

gewusst: Professionals in joinery workshops often have dozens of clamps, because you need many at once for a table top.
People say: you can never have enough clamps.

teile.einleitung: A music genre, also called a style, is a group of pieces of music with similar features. These include typical instruments, rhythms, ways of singing and often a region of origin. Countless styles have developed all over the world in this way, from tango in Argentina to yodelling in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A music genre groups together music with a similar sound, rhythm and instruments.
Reggae comes from Jamaica, samba from Brazil.
Tango developed mainly in Argentina.
The often melancholy fado comes from Portugal.
House music developed in the 1980s in Chicago.
The Schwyzerörgeli is typical of Swiss Ländler music.
When yodelling you switch quickly between chest voice and head voice.

abschnitte.text: Music is divided into genres so that you can find your way around more easily. Large areas are, for example, **classical music**, folk music, jazz, rock, pop, hip-hop and electronic music. Within these areas there are many subgroups; in rock, for example, hard rock, punk or metal. Musicians often mix several styles too, and then something new is created, which is called **crossover** or fusion.

Many styles began in the Americas. **Reggae** comes from Jamaica and became world-famous through Bob Marley; a rhythm with the stress on the offbeats is typical. **Tango** developed at the end of the 19th century mainly in Buenos Aires in Argentina; the bandoneon is typical. **Samba** from Brazil is linked to the carnival of Rio de Janeiro. Blues, jazz, country, rock 'n' roll and hip-hop come from the USA.

Electronic dance music is made mainly with synthesisers, drum machines and computers. In the 1980s **house** developed in Chicago, and at about the same time techno in Detroit. This music usually has an even, pounding beat. Since 1992 the **Street Parade** has taken place in Zurich, one of the largest techno parades in the world.

Every country has its own folk music. In Portugal people sing **fado**, an often melancholy song that tells of longing and is accompanied by the guitar. In Ireland you hear the fiddle and the flute, in Spain flamenco with guitar, singing and clapping. Fado and tango have been recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The best-known Swiss folk music is **Ländler music**, played by small bands with Schwyzerörgeli, clarinet, piano and double bass. When **yodelling** you switch quickly between a low chest voice and a high head voice, often without words. Other traditions are alphorn playing, the hammered dulcimer from the Appenzell region and natural yodelling. Every few years thousands of yodellers, alphorn players and flag throwers meet at the Federal Yodelling Festival.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a type or style of music.
Singing with a quick switch between chest voice and head voice.
Swiss folk dance and folk music in three-four time.
A squeezebox instrument that is typical of tango.

gewusst: Yodelling does not only exist in the Alps; peoples in Central Africa also know similar songs.
Bob Marley is one of the best-known musicians in the world, even though he lived to be only 36.
Every year the Street Parade in Zurich draws hundreds of thousands of people to the lake.

teile.einleitung: Wax crayons are among the first drawing tools that children use. They are made mainly of wax and colour powder. With them you can not only draw, but also try out exciting techniques.
wichtigste: Wax crayons are made of wax mixed with colour powder.
When warm they become soft and can melt.
With the long side of the crayon you can quickly colour large areas.
In frottage you rub off the patterns of objects.
Wax repels watercolour, which lets you make secret pictures.
In a scratch picture you scratch bright colours free from under a black layer.

abschnitte.text: A wax crayon is made of **wax**, for example paraffin or beeswax, and **colour pigments**. These are fine colour powders. The liquid wax is mixed with the pigments and poured into moulds. When it cools, it becomes solid. Because wax gets soft when warm, you should not leave crayons lying in the hot sun.

In **frottage** you lay a sheet of paper on an object with a texture, such as a leaf, a coin or wood. Then you rub over it with the side of the wax crayon. The fine veins of the leaf or the grain of the wood appear on the paper. The word comes from the French “frotter”, which means “to rub”. The artist **Max Ernst** made this technique known in art.

Wax and water do not mix. If you paint watercolour over a wax drawing, the paint rolls off the wax. The drawing stays visible, and the paper all around becomes coloured. With a **white wax crayon** on white paper you can draw a **secret picture** in this way. You only see it when you paint over it.

For a **scratch picture** you first colour a sheet of paper thickly with bright wax crayons. Then you cover everything with black paint or black wax. With a wooden stick or a paper clip you then scratch lines into the black layer. The bright colours appear underneath. This makes glowing pictures that can look like fireworks at night.

gewusst: The company Caran d’Ache in Geneva has been making crayons and colouring pencils for many decades.
Because wax crayons are thick and sturdy, they rarely break and sit well in small hands.

teile.einleitung: Vanitas is a Latin word meaning “vanity” or “emptiness”. In art it stands for pictures that remind us that all things pass away. The vanitas still lifes of the 17th century are especially well known.
wichtigste: Vanitas means “vanity”, “emptiness” or “empty show”.
Vanitas pictures show that nothing in the world lasts for ever.
Typical signs are skulls, hourglasses, snuffed-out candles and wilted flowers.
Vanitas still lifes were especially popular in the Netherlands in the 17th century.
A related Latin saying is “memento mori”.

abschnitte.text: The term comes from the Bible. The Book of Ecclesiastes says “Vanitas vanitatum”, roughly “Everything is vanity and passes away”. Vanitas pictures are meant to remind people that wealth, beauty and fame do not last for ever. They ask viewers to think about their own lives. The saying **“memento mori”** means “Remember that you must die”.

In a vanitas still life, almost every object has a meaning. The **skull** stands for death. An **hourglass** or pocket watch shows that time is running out. A **snuffed-out candle**, wilted flowers and rotting fruit show that everything passes. Soap bubbles also appear, because they burst in an instant.

Vanitas still lifes were most popular in the **Baroque** period, especially in the Netherlands. Many were made in the city of Leiden. The painters often also showed precious things, such as books, musical instruments, jewellery and coins. These stand for knowledge and wealth, which you cannot take with you. The pictures are usually painted very finely and precisely.

gewusst: Modern artists still take up the vanitas theme today, for example with skulls in sculptures and photos.

teile.einleitung: Polyester is a synthetic fibre made from plastic. Many sports clothes, jackets and fleece jumpers are made of it. The plastic is usually made from crude oil.
wichtigste: Polyester is a man-made fibre made of plastic.
Its raw material is mainly crude oil.
Polyester is the most widely used synthetic fibre in the world.
It is tear-resistant, hardly creases and dries quickly.
In the burn test, polyester melts into a hard bead.
Polyester fibres can be made from old PET bottles.

abschnitte.text: Polyester is one of the **man-made fibres**, which do not grow in nature. First a plastic is made from **crude oil**. This is melted and pressed through fine nozzles. This produces long, thin threads that are made into yarn. The polyester fibre was invented in England in the 1940s.

Polyester is very **tear-resistant** and keeps its shape. It hardly creases and absorbs only a little water. That is why it dries quickly, which is practical for sports clothes. On the other hand, you can sweat more easily in it than in cotton. Polyester is often mixed with natural fibres to combine the advantages of both.

With a **burn test** you can tell fibres apart, of course only with an adult and with care. If you hold a polyester fibre in a flame, it **melts**. Afterwards a hard bead is left that you cannot crush. Cotton, on the other hand, burns to soft ash, and wool smells of burnt hair.

The plastic of **PET bottles** is a polyester. In Switzerland PET bottles are collected, and some of them are turned into new fibres, for example for fleece jackets. One problem is **microplastics**: during washing, tiny fibres come loose and can get into the waste water. In addition, polyester breaks down only very slowly in nature.

gewusst: PET is short for polyethylene terephthalate, one of the most common polyesters.
Worldwide more polyester is produced than any other textile fibre, even more than cotton.

teile.einleitung: Music production is the whole journey from the idea to the finished song that you can stream or buy. It includes recording the instruments and voices, editing, mixing and finally mastering. In the past you needed an expensive recording studio for this; today many musicians also produce at home with a laptop.
wichtigste: A production includes recording, editing, mixing and mastering.
DAW stands for Digital Audio Workstation, a music program on the computer.
An equaliser changes the volume of individual frequency ranges.
A compressor reduces the dynamic range of a signal.
With panning you set the position of a sound in the stereo image.
Mastering is the last step before release.
The guitarist Les Paul is regarded as a pioneer of multitrack recording.

abschnitte.text: First, voices and instruments are recorded with **microphones**. There are dynamic microphones, which are robust, and sensitive condenser microphones. Condenser microphones need power, usually **phantom power** at 48 volts, which comes via the mixing desk or an audio interface. Electronic instruments and synthesisers can also be recorded directly without a microphone.

Today recording is mostly done with a **DAW**, a Digital Audio Workstation. Well-known programs include Ableton Live, Logic Pro and Pro Tools. Each instrument gets its own **track**, which can be changed separately. We owe this multitrack technique partly to the guitarist Les Paul, who was already layering several recordings on top of each other in the 1940s and 1950s.

During **mixing** all the tracks are combined into a whole. You set the volumes and spread the sounds to the left and right in the stereo image with **panning**. With the equaliser you change specific frequency ranges, for example more bass or less hiss. A compressor makes loud passages quieter so that everything sounds more even, and reverb makes a recording sound as if it had been made in a large room.

**Mastering** is the last editing step. The finished stereo mix is optimised for release so that it sounds good on a mobile phone, headphones and a big sound system. For streaming services loudness is measured in **LUFS**. The platforms adjust songs to a similar loudness so that you do not have to change the volume for every song.

abschnitte.titel: From the studio to the bedroom
abschnitte.text: In the past records were made in large studios such as Abbey Road Studios in London, where the Beatles recorded. Today a laptop, an audio interface, a microphone and good headphones are often enough; this is called **home recording**. Many well-known pop songs of recent years were produced wholly or partly at home. If you want to learn music production, in Switzerland you can, for example, train as a sound engineer or study at a university.

begriffe.erklaerung: Digital Audio Workstation, a program for recording and editing music.
A tool with which you make the treble, mid-range and bass louder or quieter separately.
An effect that brings loud and quiet passages closer together.
The final polish so that a song sounds good everywhere.
Spreading a sound between the left and right loudspeaker.

gewusst: In 1967 the Beatles recorded their album “Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band” with only four tracks.
Les Paul did not only invent recording techniques; a famous electric guitar still bears his name today.
A professional mixing desk can have hundreds of faders and knobs.

teile.einleitung: Joining techniques are about how to connect separate parts firmly together. In handicraft lessons, furniture making and technology there are many ways of doing this. A distinction is made mainly between detachable and permanent joints.
wichtigste: Detachable joints can be taken apart again without destroying any parts.
A screwed joint is a typical example of a detachable joint.
Rivets, gluing, welding and soldering make permanent joints.
Wood is often joined with glue, screws, nails or dowels.
The right joint depends on the material and the purpose.

abschnitte.text: A **detachable joint** can be opened and closed again. The best example is the **screw**: you unscrew it and later screw it back in. Plug connections, clips and Velcro also belong to this group. Detachable joints are practical if you want to repair, dismantle or transport something. That is why a lot of self-assembly furniture is screwed together.

A **permanent joint** holds for good. If you want to separate the parts, you have to break something. This includes **rivets**, **gluing** with glue and **welding**, in which metal melts at the joint. In **soldering**, metal parts are joined with melted solder, often made of tin. This is needed, for example, for electronic circuits.

There are special joints for wood. **Glue** is very common in handicraft lessons, but it needs time to dry. With wooden **dowels** you can join boards invisibly. Joiners also know elaborate joints such as the mortise and tenon or the dovetail, in which the parts fit exactly into each other. Joints like this often hold without any nails at all.

In technology, joints are distinguished by why they hold. In a **form-fit** joint, the parts interlock, as with jigsaw pieces. In a **force-fit** joint, friction and pressure hold, for example with a clamp or a screw. In a **material bond**, the materials themselves join together, as in gluing or welding. Engineers choose the joint according to how much load it has to bear.

gewusst: The Eiffel Tower in Paris is held together by millions of rivets.
Some old wooden houses and roof frames are built entirely without metal nails.

teile.einleitung: Nicéphore Niépce was a French inventor and is seen as one of the inventors of photography. Around 1826 he created the oldest surviving photograph in the world. It shows the view from a window of his house at Le Gras.
wichtigste: Nicéphore Niépce lived in France from 1765 to 1833.
Around 1826 he created the oldest surviving photograph, the “View from the Window at Le Gras”.
He exposed a pewter plate coated with bitumen for many hours.
He called his process **heliography**, meaning “sun drawing”.
Later he worked together with Louis Daguerre.
After his death, Daguerre developed the process further into the daguerreotype.

abschnitte.text: Nicéphore Niépce was born in 1765 in **Chalon-sur-Saône** in France. He was interested in many technical inventions. Together with his brother he even built an early engine for a boat. But one question especially occupied him: can you capture a picture made by light? For many years he carried out **experiments** on this.

Around **1826** Niépce made his breakthrough. He set up a **camera obscura**, a pinhole camera, at the window of his house at **Le Gras**. Inside it was a pewter plate coated with a kind of bitumen, like asphalt. The light made the bitumen hard in the bright areas. After washing, a picture of the roofs and buildings outside the window was left behind.

Niépce called his process **heliography**. This means “sun drawing”, from the Greek word “helios” for sun. The exposure took many hours. That is why the buildings in the picture seem to be lit from both sides, because the sun had moved on in the meantime. The picture is blurred, but it is the **oldest surviving photograph** in the world.

In 1829 Niépce began working with the painter **Louis Daguerre**. Together they wanted to improve the process. Niépce died in 1833 before they reached their goal. Daguerre developed the method further and presented the **daguerreotype** in 1839. With this, photography began to spread all over the world.

gewusst: The oldest surviving photograph is now kept in a museum in Texas.
The exposure for Niépce’s picture took so long that people could not have appeared in it at all.

teile.einleitung: ProLitteris is a Swiss collecting society based in Zurich. It makes sure that authors, visual artists and photographers receive money when their works are copied or used again. There are separate societies for music and films.
wichtigste: ProLitteris manages copyright in texts, visual art and photography.
It is based in Zurich and organised as a cooperative.
Suisa is responsible for music, Suissimage for audiovisual works.
Schools and companies, for example, pay fees for photocopies.
The money is distributed to the authors and artists.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who writes a book, paints a picture or takes a photo is the **author** of the work. **Copyright** means that others may not simply use the work however they like. But a single artist cannot check everywhere who is copying pages from her book. That is why there are **collecting societies**: they collect fees and distribute the money to their members. ProLitteris does this for literature, visual art and photography.

Schools, libraries, companies and public offices copy texts and pictures every day. For this they pay a **remuneration**, which is set out in tariffs. ProLitteris collects these amounts and distributes them to authors, publishers, artists and photographers. ProLitteris can also manage the rights when a work of art is resold or shown in a book. In this way the authors receive pay for their work.

In Switzerland there are several collecting societies with clearly separate tasks. **Suisa** looks after music, **Suissimage** films and other audiovisual works. ProLitteris is responsible for texts and pictures. The societies need a licence from the federal government and are supervised by it. The basis is the Federal Act on Copyright.

gewusst: In Switzerland copyright in a work usually ends 70 years after the death of its author.

teile.einleitung: A musical instrument is an object with which you deliberately produce notes and sounds. There are thousands of different instruments all over the world, from the simple drum to the huge church organ. They are divided into groups depending on how the sound is produced.
wichtigste: Instruments are divided into groups such as wind, string, percussion and keyboard instruments.
You make a wind instrument sound by blowing into it.
Percussion instruments are played with the hands or with beaters.
The harp belongs to the string instruments.
With the harmonica you blow and suck air through it.
Typical Swiss instruments are the alphorn, the hammered dulcimer and the Schwyzerörgeli.
Electronic instruments such as the synthesiser produce sounds with electricity.

abschnitte.text: Every note is made by a **vibration** that sets the air in motion. On a guitar a string vibrates, on a trumpet the lips and the column of air in the tube, on a drum a stretched skin. A **soundbox**, such as the hollow body of a violin, makes the sound louder and more beautiful. Experts often classify instruments by the part that vibrates, as the researchers Hornbostel and Sachs proposed in 1914.

With **wind instruments** you make the air inside vibrate by blowing into them. A distinction is made between woodwind instruments such as the recorder, flute, clarinet and oboe and brass instruments such as the trumpet, trombone and tuba. By the way, the flute counts as a woodwind instrument, even though today it is usually made of metal. The little harmonica is a wind instrument too: you blow air into it and suck it out.

On **string instruments** stretched strings vibrate. You can bow them, as with the violin, viola, cello and double bass, pluck them, as with the guitar and harp, or strike them. On the piano you press keys and small hammers strike the strings, so it is also a keyboard instrument. The organ is a **keyboard instrument** as well, but on it pipes sound.

You play **percussion instruments** by striking them with your hands, sticks or beaters. They include drums, timpani, cymbals, the triangle and the xylophone. Some, like the xylophone, have a fixed pitch; others, like the snare drum, produce more of a noise. The drum kit in a band combines several drums and cymbals. A Swiss instrument from Bern is the **Hang**, a sound bowl made of steel that was invented in 2000.

The **alphorn** is a very long wooden instrument, often more than three metres long, which herdsmen used in the past to communicate in the mountains. On the **hammered dulcimer**, which is especially popular in the Appenzell region, you strike strings with small hammers. The **Schwyzerörgeli** is a small accordion that appeared at the end of the 19th century in Central Switzerland and is very popular in folk music. Drums and piccolos also play a big role at the Basel carnival.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hollow part of an instrument that amplifies the sound.
A wind instrument on which keys or holes change the pitch, such as the flute or clarinet.
A wind instrument on which the lips vibrate in the mouthpiece, such as the trumpet.
An electronic instrument that produces sounds with electricity.

gewusst: The largest organs in the world have over 20000 pipes.
An alphorn has no keys or holes; the notes are produced only by the tension of the lips.
The theremin is played without touching it, just by moving your hands in the air.

teile.einleitung: We come across paper every day: in exercise books, books, packaging and when making things. It is made of fine fibres that are pressed into thin sheets. Used paper can be collected and turned into new paper.
wichtigste: Today paper is mostly made from wood fibres.
The fibres are mixed with lots of water into a pulp, pressed and dried.
Paper was invented in China.
Waste paper is collected and made into new paper.
Wet paper becomes soft and tears easily.
Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding.

abschnitte.text: To make paper you need **fibres**, mostly from wood. The wood is broken up and turned into **pulp** or ground wood. The fibres then float in a great deal of water as a thin mush. On a sieve the water drains away, and the fibres mat together into a layer. This is pressed and dried until a firm sheet forms.

Paper was invented about 2,000 years ago in **China**. From there it came to Europe through the Arab world. Before that, people wrote, for example, on **papyrus** made from a plant or on parchment made from animal skin. The word paper comes from papyrus. With printing, paper became more and more important in Europe.

**Waste paper** is used paper, for example newspapers, brochures or cardboard boxes. In Switzerland people tie it into bundles and put it out for the paper collection, which is often organised by municipalities, schools or clubs. At the paper mill the old fibres are broken down again and made into new paper. This needs less wood, water and energy. But it cannot be done entirely without fresh fibres, because the fibres get shorter each time.

The fibres in paper hold on to each other. If **water** gets between them, these bonds come apart. The paper becomes soft, goes wavy and tears easily. That is why some papers are specially treated so that they can cope better with moisture, for example kitchen roll or paper for watercolour paintings.

In **origami** from Japan you fold animals, flowers or boats without scissors or glue. **Coloured paper** comes in many colours for cutting and gluing. For **papier-mâché** you stick strips of paper with paste layer by layer onto a shape, for example a balloon, and let everything dry. **Tracing paper** lets a lot of light through, so you can use it to trace pictures.

gewusst: A sheet of A4 measures 21 by 29.7 centimetres.
A sheet of A0 is exactly one square metre, and A4 is one sixteenth of it.

teile.einleitung: Music is much more than beautiful sounds: it brings people together and plays an important role in every society. You hear it at celebrations, in churches, at demonstrations, in stadiums and at festivals. Music can show which group you belong to, and it has often made history too.
wichtigste: There is no known human culture without music.
The Woodstock Festival of 1969 became the symbol of an entire youth movement.
Jazz began around 1900 in New Orleans, hip-hop in the 1970s in the Bronx in New York.
In Switzerland the cooperative SUISA manages the copyrights of music creators.
Since 2012 music education has been part of Article 67a of the Federal Constitution.
The Swiss Psalm has officially been the national anthem of Switzerland since 1981.
Claude Nobs shaped the Montreux Jazz Festival, founded in 1967.

abschnitte.text: People have been making music for tens of thousands of years to celebrate, to mourn or to pray together. Singing or making music together strengthens the **sense of community**, for example in a choir, a village band or a football stadium. Anthems stand for a country: the **Swiss Psalm** has officially been the national anthem of Switzerland since 1981. Young people, too, often show with their favourite music which scene they belong to.

Music can express opinions and move people to act. In the USA songs played an important role in the civil rights movement of the 1960s. The **Woodstock Festival** in August 1969, with hundreds of thousands of visitors, became a symbol of peace and the youth culture of that time. Jazz, which began around 1900 in New Orleans, and hip-hop from the **Bronx** in New York were shaped above all by African American people and gave them a strong voice.

Music is also a large industry with record companies, concert promoters and streaming services. The philosophers Theodor W. Adorno and Max Horkheimer criticised the industrial mass production of culture and called it the **culture industry**. Anyone who composes music or writes song lyrics holds a **copyright** in it. In Switzerland the cooperative SUISA makes sure that composers, lyricists and music publishers receive money when their music is played on the radio, at a concert or on the internet.

In Switzerland children learn to sing, read music and clap rhythms in music lessons. Many also go to a **music school** and learn an instrument there. In 2012 the voters accepted a new article on music education, **Article 67a** of the Federal Constitution. It obliges the Confederation and the cantons to promote music in schools and music schools.

Switzerland has a lively festival culture. The **Montreux Jazz Festival** was founded in 1967 and run for decades by Claude Nobs; world stars such as Miles Davis and Deep Purple performed there. Other well-known festivals are the Paléo Festival in Nyon, the Openair St Gallen and the Gurtenfestival in Bern. In many villages, music societies and yodelling clubs are also important associations.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right that a work belongs to the person who created it.
A Swiss cooperative that collects money for music creators when their works are used.
A critical term for culture that is mass-produced like goods in factories.
A solemn song that stands, for example, for a country.

gewusst: There were so many people on the Woodstock festival site that in the end the organisers gave up checking tickets.
The song “Smoke on the Water” by Deep Purple tells of a fire at the casino in Montreux in 1971.
The melody of the Swiss Psalm was written by a monk, Father Alberik Zwyssig.

teile.einleitung: The rasp is a tool that is similar to a file, but has coarse teeth that stand individually. It is used mainly to remove wood quickly and shape it. Afterwards the surface is smoothed with a file and sandpaper.
wichtigste: The rasp has coarse teeth that stand individually.
It removes a lot of material at once.
It is used mainly for wood.
After the rasp, you smooth with a file and sandpaper.
There are flat, half-round and round rasps.

abschnitte.text: A rasp and a file look similar. On a **file**, the grooves are cut in rows and are rather fine. The **rasp**, on the other hand, has lots of separate, pointed **teeth** that are punched into the metal one by one. That is why it bites harder and removes more wood. But the surface becomes rough as it does so.

You clamp the workpiece firmly in a workbench or a vice. You hold the rasp by the **handle** with one hand and guide the front with the other. The work is done mainly on the **forward stroke**; when pulling back, you lift slightly. With the flat side you work on straight and curved surfaces, with the round side on curves and holes. Finally come the file and **sandpaper**.

Rasps are not only needed by joiners and sculptors. The **farrier** also uses a large rasp to bring horses’ hooves into shape. At school, rasps are used in handicraft lessons, for example for wooden figures or wooden spoons.

gewusst: Rasps get clogged with wood shavings; you clean them with a wire brush.

teile.einleitung: In sewing you join pieces of fabric with a needle and thread. You can sew by hand or with a sewing machine. With a few simple stitches you can already make bags, cushions or soft toys.
wichtigste: The small hole in a sewing needle is called the **eye**.
A **thimble** protects your finger when sewing by hand.
A knot at the end of the thread stops the thread slipping through the fabric.
The line where two pieces of fabric are sewn together is called a **seam**.
In **running stitch** the needle goes alternately up and down.
In **cross stitch** two slanting stitches form an X.
Pieces of fabric are pinned together with **pins** before sewing.

abschnitte.text: To sew by hand you need a **sewing needle**, thread, fabric and scissors. The needle has a point at one end and a small hole at the other, the **eye**. You thread the thread through the eye. A **thimble** on your middle finger helps you push the needle through the fabric without pricking yourself. **Pins** with small heads hold the pieces of fabric in place.

First you thread the needle. You tie a **knot** at the end. It is thicker than the hole in the fabric, so the thread catches at the first stitch. Then you pin the pieces of fabric together so that nothing slips. Now you can start sewing. At the end you fasten off the thread with a few small stitches and a knot.

The simplest stitch is **running stitch**. You push the needle up and down at equal distances. This makes a dashed line. In **cross stitch** you first sew a slanting stitch and then cross it with a second one. This makes a small X. With lots of cross stitches you can embroider whole pictures.

Where two pieces of fabric are joined with stitches, a **seam** is formed. On clothes you can see seams, for example, at the sides or on the sleeves. They are usually on the inside, so that you can hardly see them from outside. With a **sewing machine** sewing goes much faster. It moves the needle up and down very quickly and makes long, even seams.

gewusst: The oldest sewing needles in the world were made of bone and are tens of thousands of years old.
In the subject of textile design, children in Switzerland learn to sew as early as primary school.

teile.einleitung: A Pietà is a picture or sculpture showing Mary with the dead Jesus Christ on her lap. The word is Italian and means “piety” or “pity”. The most famous Pietà was made by Michelangelo for St Peter’s Basilica in Rome.
wichtigste: A Pietà shows the mourning Mary with the dead Christ on her lap.
Pietà is Italian and means “piety” or “pity”.
In German-speaking countries such figures are also called Vesperbild.
The best-known Pietà was made by Michelangelo from marble around 1499.
It stands in St Peter’s Basilica in Rome.

abschnitte.text: A **Pietà** shows a scene from Christian tradition. After the crucifixion, Mary holds her dead son Jesus on her lap and mourns him. Images like this were meant to move believers to feel with her and to reflect. In German-speaking countries they are also called **Vesperbild**, because the scene was remembered at the evening prayer, vespers. Pietà figures can still be found in many churches today, in Switzerland too.

The most famous Pietà was made by the Italian artist **Michelangelo** around 1499 from a single block of white **marble**. He was only about 24 years old at the time. The figures look very lifelike, and the folds of the robe look almost like real fabric. Mary looks strikingly young and calm. The sculpture stands in **St Peter’s Basilica** in Rome and is the only work on which Michelangelo carved his name.

In 1972 a man damaged the Pietà in St Peter’s with a hammer. Restorers carefully put the broken-off pieces back together. Since then the sculpture has stood behind a protective glass wall. Michelangelo later made other Pietà figures; his last one remained unfinished and is now in Milan.

gewusst: Michelangelo carved his name on a band running across Mary’s chest.
He was still working on his last Pietà, the Rondanini Pietà, a few days before his death.

teile.einleitung: The font size says how big a typeface is. In word processing programs you choose it as a number, for example 12. It is measured in typographic points.
wichtigste: The font size is the size of a typeface.
It is given in typographic points.
A DTP point measures 1/72 of an inch, about 0.353 mm.
For body text, 10 to 12 point is often used.
Font size dates back to the time of hot metal type.

abschnitte.text: In **hot metal type**, every letter stood on a small block of metal called the **body**. The font size referred to the height of this body. That is why a letter in 12 point is usually smaller than 12 points, because a little space is left above and below. Two typefaces with the same font size can therefore look different in size.

In the past there were different point measurements, for example the **Didot point**. With **desktop publishing**, designing on the computer, the DTP point became standard. It measures exactly 1/72 of an inch. As an inch is 25.4 mm long, that comes to about 0.353 mm. So a typeface in 72 point is about one inch tall.

For letters and schoolwork, people often choose 11 or 12 point. **Footnotes** are smaller, headings bigger. On posters you need very large font sizes so that people can read them from far away. A text is easy to read when font size, line length and line spacing fit together.

gewusst: The typographic point system was developed in the 18th century by French type founders such as Pierre Simon Fournier and François-Ambroise Didot.

teile.einleitung: Net art is art that was created for the internet and only works there. It began in the 1990s, when the World Wide Web was new. Browsers, links and websites are the artists’ material.
wichtigste: Net art began in the 1990s.
It is also called **net.art**.
The works use browsers, links and websites as their material.
Many works react to the visitors.
The Swiss group **etoy** was among the well-known net artists.
Because technology changes quickly, net art is hard to preserve.

abschnitte.text: In the mid-1990s the **World Wide Web** became available to many people. Some artists began to create works that only function on the internet. This is called **net art** or **net.art**. The works are not pictures that you can simply hang on the wall. You visit them in the **browser** and click your way through them.

Net artists play with what makes the internet what it is: **links**, windows, program code and error messages. Some works tell stories in which you choose the path yourself by clicking. Others look chaotic on purpose, as if the computer were broken. Many works are **interactive** and change because of the visitors. They are often also about questions of communication and technology.

A well-known group was **etoy**, founded in Switzerland. The members appeared like a company, with matching clothes and invented names. Around 1999 etoy had a dispute with an American toy shop about the name of their internet address. Many people on the internet supported the artists. This dispute itself became a famous net art project.

abschnitte.titel: How do you preserve net art?
abschnitte.text: The internet changes very quickly. Old programs no longer run, websites disappear and browsers display pages differently. That is why it is difficult to **preserve** net art. Some organisations collect old works and run them in rebuilt old browsers. In this way later generations can still experience early net art.

gewusst: Some early net art works only work now if you open them in a browser from the 1990s.
You can visit many net art works for free from home, without paying to enter a museum.

teile.einleitung: A still life is a picture that shows objects that do not move. Typical are fruit, flowers, glasses and jugs. This type of picture has existed for centuries.
wichtigste: A still life shows lifeless, arranged objects.
Typical are fruit, flowers, glasses and jugs.
In French it is called “nature morte”, dead nature.
In the 17th century it was especially popular in the Netherlands.
Many still lifes have a hidden meaning.

abschnitte.text: A **still life** shows things that do not move. The artist carefully lays them out beforehand; he **arranges** them. Typical are fruit, flowers, glasses, jugs, bread or books. The painter can study shapes, colours and light in peace. That is why the still life is also a good exercise for beginners.

In French it is called **“nature morte”**, that is, dead nature. In German and English, on the other hand, people speak of still life, in German “Stillleben”. The word comes from Dutch, where these pictures were very popular.

In the **17th century** Dutch artists painted countless still lifes for rich townspeople. This is called the **Golden Age** of Dutch painting. The pictures showed splendid bunches of flowers, laid tables and precious vessels. The painters reproduced every detail very precisely, for example drops of water on a flower.

Many still lifes have a **meaning**. A burnt-down candle or an hourglass reminds you that time is passing. Pictures like this are called **vanitas** still lifes, after the Latin word for transience. Later the Frenchman **Paul Cézanne** painted famous still lifes with apples. With them he wanted to show how shapes can be seen in a new way.

gewusst: Some flower still lifes show flowers that in reality never bloom at the same time. The painter put them together from studies.
Photographers also make still lifes today, for example for cookery books.

teile.einleitung: In German typesetting, “Schusterjunge” (literally “shoemaker’s boy”) is a technical term. It refers to the first line of a paragraph that stands all alone at the end of a page or column; in English this is called an orphan.
wichtigste: An orphan is a single first line of a paragraph at the bottom of a page.
The rest of the paragraph is then on the next page.
It counts as a typesetting mistake, because the paragraph is split awkwardly.
Good layout programs can avoid orphans automatically.
In English it is called an “orphan”.

abschnitte.text: A text is made up of **paragraphs**. If a paragraph begins right at the bottom of a page, it can happen that only its first line still fits. This lonely line is called an **orphan**, in German a “Schusterjunge”. The reader has to turn the page to read on. This interrupts the flow of reading and looks untidy.

Typesetters make sure that at least two lines of a paragraph stand together. You can push the line onto the next page or shorten the text slightly. Word processing programs have a setting for this, often called **widow and orphan control**. It automatically makes sure that no single lines are left at the edge of the page.

gewusst: An old saying among German typesetters goes: “A Schusterjunge does not know where he is going.”

teile.einleitung: A countersink is a tool used to work on the edge of a drilled hole. This lets a screw head, for example, sit flush instead of sticking out.
wichtigste: A countersink widens the edge of a drilled hole.
The cone countersink makes a cone-shaped recess.
A countersunk screw sits exactly flush in it.
You can also deburr drilled holes with the countersink.
You fit it into the drill.

abschnitte.text: The **cone countersink** looks like a small point with cutting edges. You put it on a finished **drilled hole** and drill in briefly. This creates a cone-shaped recess at the edge. A **countersunk screw** has a head of exactly this shape. It then fits in exactly and does not stand above the surface.

When drilling metal, sharp edges called **burrs** often form at the edge. You can remove these edges with the cone countersink; this is called **deburring**. There are also **counterbores**, which make a cylindrical recess with a flat bottom. Screws with a round, flat head disappear into them. You work slowly with the countersink and with little pressure.

gewusst: A countersunk screw head is safer, because you cannot bump into it or get caught on it.

teile.einleitung: A sewing pattern is a paper template used to cut out fabric for a piece of clothing. It contains the outlines of all the pieces and lots of markings that help with sewing. If you understand the markings, you can sew a piece of clothing that fits.
wichtigste: A sewing pattern is a paper template for the pieces of a garment.
The long arrow on a pattern piece shows the grain line.
The seam allowance is the extra edge of fabric outside the stitching line.
A piece marked “place on fold” is laid against the folded edge of the fabric.
Notches show which places belong together.
First you measure your own body measurements, for example your waist.

abschnitte.text: Before choosing a sewing pattern, you measure your own **body measurements** with a soft **tape measure**. Important ones include the chest, the hips and the **waist**. The waist is measured at the narrowest part of the body, between the ribcage and the hips. You measure loosely, not too tightly. With a size chart you then find the right size.

A long **arrow** is drawn on every pattern piece. It shows the **grain line** and must lie parallel to the firm woven edge of the fabric, the selvedge. Then the garment hangs straight and does not twist. Small lines or triangles on the edges are called **notches**. When the notches of two pieces meet, the pieces are in the right position for sewing together.

If a piece says **“place on fold”**, you fold the fabric and lay the centre line of the piece exactly against the folded edge. This creates a symmetrical piece twice as wide with no seam in the middle, for example a back piece. The **seam allowance** is the edge of fabric outside the stitching line. You need it so that you can sew the pieces together. It is often 1 to 1.5 centimetres wide.

You lay the sewing pattern on the fabric and pin it in place. Lines and markings are transferred with tailor’s chalk or with a **tracing wheel**. You run this small toothed wheel along the lines, and the dressmaker’s carbon paper underneath presses the line onto the fabric. Then you carefully cut along the cutting line with fabric scissors.

gewusst: In many shop-bought sewing patterns the pieces for several sizes lie on top of each other; you trace your own size onto tissue paper.

teile.einleitung: Sheep’s wool is the hair of sheep and one of the oldest textile fibres used by people. It keeps you warm, absorbs moisture and can be spun into yarn or made into felt. Like our hair, wool consists mainly of the protein keratin.
wichtigste: Sheep’s wool is an animal hair and a natural fibre.
It consists mainly of the protein keratin.
Wool hairs have a layer of scales.
In hot water with a lot of rubbing, the scales hook together and the wool felts.
Wool still keeps you warm when it is a little damp.
Sheep are usually shorn once or twice a year.

abschnitte.text: Once or twice a year the sheep are **shorn**. The cut-off coat is called the fleece. Then the wool is washed, because it contains dirt and **wool grease**. In carding, the fibres are combed and lined up. Finally they are twisted into a thread by **spinning**. You can knit or weave with this yarn.

Like our hair and nails, wool consists mainly of **keratin**, a protein. Under the microscope you can see lots of little **scales** on each hair, overlapping like roof tiles. The hairs are also crimped. This creates lots of air pockets between the fibres, and air holds warmth well. The wool grease, also called **lanolin**, is cleaned and used, for example, in ointments.

If you wash a woollen jumper too hot and with lots of movement, it can **felt**. Warmth, moisture and rubbing open up the scales, and they hook into each other. The fibres slide together and can no longer be separated. The fabric becomes dense, hard and smaller. That is why wool is washed cool, on the wool programme or by hand. In **felting**, exactly this effect is used on purpose, for example for slippers or craft figures.

Many sheep are kept in Switzerland, often on alpine pastures in summer. The most common breed is the **White Alpine Sheep**. The **Valais Blacknose sheep**, with its black face and twisted horns, is also well known. However, much of the Swiss wool is hardly used today, because selling it does not pay. Some businesses turn it into insulation, duvets or yarn.

gewusst: Wool can absorb a lot of water vapour before it feels wet.
In the burn test, wool smells of burnt hair, because it is hair after all.

teile.einleitung: Watercolours are paints that you thin with water and put on with a brush. At school you often paint with a paint box full of little blocks of colour. Depending on how much water you use, the colours become strong or see-through.
wichtigste: Watercolours are thinned with water and painted with a brush.
Watercolour paints are transparent and let the paper show through.
Opaque paints, on the other hand, cover the surface underneath.
When drying, watercolour usually becomes a little lighter.
You rinse the brush before every new colour.
In the wet-on-wet technique the paint spreads on wet paper.

abschnitte.text: Watercolour consists of fine colour powder, the **pigments**, and a **binder**. In watercolour paints this is often **gum arabic**, a sap from acacia trees. The binder makes the paint stick to the paper. When you thin the paint with water, it becomes lighter. Wet paint shines and looks stronger; as it dries it becomes a little lighter.

The German word **Aquarell** for watercolour comes from the Latin “aqua”, which means water. Watercolour paints are thin and **transparent**: you can see the white paper and earlier layers of paint through them. **Opaque paints**, also called gouache, contain more pigment and cover the surface underneath. With them you can paint light colours on top of dark ones. Many school paint boxes contain opaque paints.

A brush consists of the hairs, the handle and the **ferrule**. The ferrule is the little metal tube that holds the hairs in place. With a thin **round brush** you paint fine lines, with a **flat brush** wide areas. A **rag** helps you dab excess water out of the brush. Before every new colour, you rinse the brush in the water pot, otherwise the colour gets dirty.

In the **wet-on-wet technique** you first wet the paper and then dab paint onto it. The paint flows apart softly and creates gentle transitions, good for sky and water. In **glazing**, you paint a transparent layer over a dry layer. This way the colours mix on the paper. Thick painting paper is best for a lot of water, because thin paper cockles.

gewusst: In 1502 Albrecht Dürer painted his famous “Young Hare” with watercolours.
White areas in a watercolour are often not painted at all; the paper is simply left blank.

teile.einleitung: Weaving is a very old technique for making fabric out of threads. Threads stretched lengthwise and threads passed crosswise cross each other. In this way clothes, carpets, cloths and many other textiles are made.
wichtigste: In weaving, two sets of threads cross at right angles.
The threads stretched lengthwise are called warp threads.
The thread passed across is called the weft thread.
Weaving is done on a loom or a small weaving frame.
The crosswise thread runs through the shed between the warp threads.
With the beater you push the rows close together.
The selvedge is the firm edge that does not fray.

abschnitte.text: First you stretch lots of threads tightly lengthwise. These are the **warp threads**; together they are called the warp. Then you pass a crosswise thread alternately over and under the warp threads. This crosswise thread is called the **weft thread**. Together the two sets of threads form the **woven fabric**.

If you lift some of the warp threads, an opening appears, the **shed**. You pass the weft thread through this shed with a **shuttle** or a large **weaving needle**. After each row you press the thread against the previous rows with the **beater**. This makes the fabric dense and firm. At the edge the thread turns and runs back, which creates the **selvedge**.

The way the threads cross is called the **weave**. The simplest is **plain weave**: the weft thread always goes alternately over one and under one warp thread. **Twill weave** creates a diagonal pattern, like the one you know from denim. In **satin weave**, the threads lie on top for a long way, which is why the fabric shines, as with satin. With coloured threads you can weave stripes and checks.

People have been weaving for many thousands of years. In the **lakeside pile dwellings** on Swiss lakes, too, remains of fabrics made of flax, from which linen is made, have been found. At school people often weave on a small **weaving frame**. You can make a coaster or a small rug, for example. Today most fabric is made on large weaving machines in factories.

gewusst: Denim is woven in twill weave, which is why you can see fine diagonal lines on it.
The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.

teile.einleitung: Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch painter whose pictures are now among the most famous and most expensive in the world. With strong colours and thick, swirling brushstrokes he painted sunflowers, starry skies and landscapes. During his lifetime, however, he was poor and almost unknown.
wichtigste: Vincent van Gogh was born in the Netherlands in 1853.
He painted for only about ten years, but created hundreds of paintings.
Typical of him are thick, strong brushstrokes and glowing colours.
His brother Theo helped him all his life with money and letters.
He painted many of his best-known pictures in Arles in the south of France.
The “Sunflowers”, “The Starry Night” and his bedroom are famous.
The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam has the largest collection of his works.

abschnitte.text: Vincent van Gogh was born on 30 March 1853 in Groot-Zundert in the **Netherlands**. His father was a pastor. Before he became a painter, Vincent worked among other things for an art dealer and as an assistant preacher. Only at about 27 did he decide to become an artist. His early pictures such as “The Potato Eaters” are still dark and earthy.

His younger brother **Theo** was an art dealer in Paris. He regularly sent Vincent money so that he could paint. The two wrote each other hundreds of **letters**, which still survive today. In them Vincent tells what he is painting and what he is feeling. Without Theo’s help, many of the famous pictures would never have existed.

From 1886 van Gogh lived in Paris, where he got to know the bright colours of the Impressionists. In 1888 he moved to **Arles** in the south of France, where the brilliant light thrilled him. There he painted several pictures of **sunflowers** in a vase and the “Yellow House” he lived in. He also painted his **bedroom** several times. The painter Paul Gauguin visited him, but the two quarrelled fiercely.

Van Gogh suffered from a serious mental illness. That is why in 1889 and 1890 he lived in a clinic in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. From the window, in June 1889, he painted **“The Starry Night”**, with swirling stars above a village. The picture now hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Van Gogh died on 29 July 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise near Paris, aged only 37.

Van Gogh often put the paint on so thickly that you can feel the **brushstrokes**. He is one of the artists of **Post-Impressionism** and later influenced the Expressionists. During his lifetime he sold only very few pictures. Today his works fetch prices of many millions of francs at auctions.

The **Van Gogh Museum** in Amsterdam opened in 1973 and has the largest collection of his paintings and drawings. The Kröller-Müller Museum in the Netherlands also shows many works. In Switzerland you can see pictures by van Gogh, for example, in the Kunsthaus Zürich.

begriffe.erklaerung: An art movement after Impressionism with strong colours and personal expression.
A painting style that captures light and fleeting impressions with bright colours.
