The mark that a brush with paint leaves on the canvas.
A picture in which an artist paints themselves.

gewusst: Van Gogh painted more than 35 self-portraits, partly because he had no money for models.
In only about ten years he created around 860 oil paintings.
Van Gogh admired Japanese colour woodblock prints and painted copies of some of them.

teile.einleitung: A long take, also called a sequence shot, is a long film shot that shows a whole scene without a cut. Instead of jumping from picture to picture, the camera usually moves along with the characters. Shots like this are difficult to film and so are often famous.
wichtigste: A long take shows a whole scene without a single cut.
Often the camera moves through the space instead of cutting.
Everyone involved has to work together exactly, otherwise you start again from the beginning.
The opening of Orson Welles’s film “Touch of Evil” from 1958 is famous.
Some films look like a single shot but hide cuts.

abschnitte.text: A film normally consists of many short **shots** that are put together in editing. In a **long take**, on the other hand, the camera runs without a break for a whole scene. So that there is still variety, the camera travels or pans and follows the characters. The viewer experiences the action as if in real time. This often feels especially exciting and close.

For a long take everything has to be planned exactly. Actors, camera, lighting and sound have to fit together perfectly. If a mistake happens, the whole scene has to be filmed again. The **Steadicam** helps, a mount that keeps the camera steady while walking. Today small cameras and drones help too.

The opening of Orson Welles’s “Touch of Evil” from 1958 is well known: the camera follows a car through a border town for several minutes. Alfred Hitchcock filmed “Rope” from 1948 so that it looks almost like a single long shot; the few cuts are cleverly hidden. In the film “Russian Ark” from 2002, one real shot without a cut lasts the whole film.

gewusst: For “Russian Ark”, the camera wandered through the Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg in a single shot.

teile.einleitung: Music theory explains how music is built and why it sounds the way it does. It deals with notes, intervals, scales, chords, keys and rhythm. If you know some music theory, you understand pieces of music better and find it easier to compose or improvise yourself.
wichtigste: An interval is the distance between two notes.
A perfect fifth spans seven semitones.
Inverting a major third gives a minor sixth.
A major has three sharps in its key signature; the relative key of E flat major is C minor.
The tritone is an augmented fourth.
A perfect octave has the frequency ratio 2:1.
The standard ISO 16 sets the concert pitch a¹ at 440 Hz.
A syncopation shifts the stress onto a beat that would normally be unstressed.

abschnitte.text: The distance between two notes is called an **interval**. The names come from Latin: unison, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh and octave. A perfect fifth spans seven semitones, an octave twelve. If you invert an interval by moving the lower note up an octave, a major third, for example, becomes a minor sixth. The **tritone**, an augmented fourth, sounds especially tense and used to be called “diabolus in musica” (the devil in music).

Every note has a **frequency**, which says how many times it vibrates per second. In a perfect octave the higher note vibrates exactly twice as fast, so the ratio is 2:1. In a perfect fifth it is 3:2. The Greek scholar Pythagoras already studied such ratios on strings. So that everyone tunes the same way, the standard ISO 16 sets the **concert pitch** a¹ at 440 hertz, but many orchestras tune slightly higher.

A **key** such as C major or A minor determines which notes set the tone in a piece. At the beginning of the music, the key signature shows which notes are raised or lowered: G major has one sharp, A major three sharps, E flat major three flats. Every major key has a **relative minor** with the same key signature; C minor belongs to E flat major. The **circle of fifths** arranges all the keys clearly in a circle.

Besides major and minor there are older scales, called **church modes** or modes. Their names, such as Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian and Mixolydian, come from regions of ancient Greece. Mixolydian is like a major scale with a minor seventh and often appears in rock and folk music. Dorian sounds like minor with a bright sixth and is popular in jazz.

If you play several notes at the same time, you get a **chord**. The most important one is the triad made of the root, the third and the fifth, for example C, E and G. Music theory also includes rhythm, with bars, note values and stresses. A **syncopation** shifts the stress onto a beat that would normally be unstressed, which makes jazz, pop and funk especially lively.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between two notes, for example a third or a fifth.
The note a¹ to which instruments are tuned, usually 440 Hz.
A minor key and a major key with the same key signature, such as C major and A minor.
A circle in which all the keys are arranged a fifth apart.
Stress on a beat that would normally be unstressed.

gewusst: The first two notes of the theme tune of “The Simpsons” form a tritone.
Today many orchestras tune to 442 or 443 Hz because it sounds a little more brilliant.
According to a legend, Pythagoras discovered the number ratios of notes in a smithy while listening to the sound of hammers.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss railway clock hangs in almost every SBB station. With its black bars and red signal disc, it is an icon of Swiss design.
wichtigste: The engineer Hans Hilfiker designed the clock in 1944.
It has black bars instead of numbers.
The red second hand with its disc was added in 1953.
It is reminiscent of a station master’s signalling disc.
Every minute, the second hand waits briefly at the twelve.
The clock is seen all over the world as an example of good design.

abschnitte.text: **Hans Hilfiker** worked as an engineer for the SBB. In 1944 he designed a clock that could be read easily even from a long distance. Instead of numbers, the white dial shows bold **black bars**. The hour and minute hands are simple black bars. Everything unnecessary was left out.

In 1953 the clock got its red **second hand**. It ends in a round disc and is reminiscent of the signalling disc a station master used to send a train on its way. This hand makes the clock unmistakable. It is also the first thing many people notice.

The second hand goes round a little faster than one minute. At the twelve it stops briefly and waits for a signal from a **master clock**. Only then does the minute hand jump on, and all the clocks in the network run in step again. In this way all the station clocks in Switzerland show the same time.

The railway clock is shown in design museums. It is also available as a **wristwatch** and as a wall clock for the home. The SBB protects the design as its trademark. For many people the clock stands for Swiss **punctuality**.

gewusst: In 2012 a large technology company had to pay the SBB a licence fee because it had used the clock’s design in an app.
Today the clock can also be found in stations outside Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Renaissance is an era of European art and culture from about 1400 to 1600. The French word means “rebirth”, because at that time people rediscovered the art and knowledge of the ancient Greeks and Romans. Some of the most famous works of art in the world were created in this period.
wichtigste: Renaissance means “rebirth” in French.
The era began around 1400 in Italy, especially in the city of Florence.
Artists took the art of ancient times as their model.
With linear perspective, pictures suddenly looked spacious and deep.
Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael are the best-known artists of the High Renaissance.
Rich families such as the Medici paid artists for their works.
People and nature moved to the centre of attention.

abschnitte.text: The Renaissance followed the **Middle Ages** and lasted roughly from 1400 to 1600. Scholars read the writings of the ancient Greeks and Romans again. This way of thinking is called **humanism**, because people are at its centre. Artists studied ancient statues and buildings and took them as models. The movement spread from Italy across the whole of Europe.

The cradle of the Renaissance was **Florence** in Tuscany. The rich banking family of the **Medici** supported many artists and scholars there. The master builder Filippo Brunelleschi built the huge dome of Florence Cathedral, which was consecrated in 1436. Around 1485 Sandro Botticelli painted “The Birth of Venus” in Florence, in which the goddess stands on a shell.

An important invention of the Renaissance was **linear perspective**. In it, all the lines that lead into the depth run towards a **vanishing point**. This makes a flat picture look like a view into a real room. Brunelleschi carried out experiments on this at the beginning of the 15th century, and many painters took up the technique.

**Leonardo da Vinci** painted the Mona Lisa and the wall painting “The Last Supper” in Milan. He was also an inventor, researcher and engineer. **Michelangelo** created the marble statue “David” in Florence, more than five metres tall. From 1508 to 1512 he painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican. There **Raphael** painted the large fresco “The School of Athens” with many ancient philosophers.

There were Renaissance artists north of the Alps too. **Albrecht Dürer** from Nuremberg travelled to Italy and in 1502 painted the famous watercolour “Young Hare”. Hans Holbein the Younger worked for a long time in **Basel** and painted portraits and wall paintings there. The scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam also lived in Basel, where many books were printed at that time.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type. As a result, the new ideas spread much faster. The Renaissance was also the time of great voyages of discovery and new research. Its works of art still draw millions of people to Italy every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A way of thinking that puts people and the knowledge of ancient times at the centre.
The time of the ancient Greeks and Romans.
A wall painting that is painted on fresh, still damp plaster.
A point in a picture towards which all lines going into the depth run.

gewusst: Leonardo da Vinci wrote many of his notes in mirror writing, from right to left.
Michelangelo painted much of the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel standing on high scaffolding with his head tilted back.
Michelangelo’s David was carved from a single block of marble that other sculptors had given up on before.

teile.einleitung: Colours can seem warm or cold, although of course they have no real temperature. Red, orange and yellow remind us of fire and the sun, blue and turquoise of ice and water. Artists use this effect to paint moods.
wichtigste: Warm colours are mainly red, orange and yellow.
Cold colours are mainly blue, turquoise and blue-green.
Warm colours remind us of fire and the sun, cold ones of ice and water.
Winter or a glacier is often painted with cold colours.
A room painted red or orange feels warm and cosy.
From about 1901 to 1904 Picasso painted almost only in shades of blue.

abschnitte.text: On the **colour wheel**, you can divide the colours into two halves. On one side are the **warm colours** yellow, orange and red. On the other side are the **cold colours** blue, turquoise and blue-green. Green and violet lie in between and can seem warmer or cooler depending on the mixture. A red with a little blue, for example, looks cooler than a red with a little yellow.

Our experience shapes how we feel about colours. **Fire**, embers and the **sun** glow yellow, orange and red. That is why these colours seem warm, lively and strong. **Ice**, snow, cold water and the winter sky look blue and white. That is why blue and turquoise seem cool, fresh and calm.

With warm and cold colours you can paint moods. You paint a **campfire** with red, orange and yellow, a **glacier** with blue, white and turquoise. Warm colours seem to come forward, cold ones seem to move back. That is why distant mountains often look bluish in pictures. The opposition is called the **cold-warm contrast**. The Swiss art teacher **Johannes Itten** described it as one of seven colour contrasts.

From about 1901 to 1904 the Spanish painter **Pablo Picasso** painted almost only with shades of blue. This time is called his **Blue Period**. His pictures from this time seem sad, cool and quiet. After that he painted with warmer pink and orange tones; this time is called the Rose Period. This shows well how strongly colours change the mood of a picture.

gewusst: Johannes Itten was born in the canton of Bern and taught at the Bauhaus in Germany.
Many people judge a room painted blue to be cooler than a red one, even though the temperature is the same.

teile.einleitung: The sewing machine sews much faster and more evenly than by hand. It works with two threads, the top thread and the bobbin thread, which loop together in the fabric. It was invented in the 19th century, and Switzerland also has a well-known sewing machine brand.
wichtigste: The **top thread** comes from the reel of thread, the **bobbin thread** from the bobbin under the needle plate.
The basic stitch is called **lockstitch**.
**Zigzag stitch** is used to neaten the edges of fabric.
The **feed dogs** push the fabric along stitch by stitch.
On a machine needle, the eye is close to the point.
In 1830 Barthélemy Thimonnier received a patent for a sewing machine in France.
The Swiss company Bernina comes from Steckborn in the canton of Thurgau.

abschnitte.text: The **top thread** runs from the reel through several guides to the needle. The **bobbin thread** is wound on a small **bobbin**. It sits under the **needle plate** in the **hook**. The **presser foot** presses the fabric down. Underneath are the **feed dogs** with toothed bars. They move and push the fabric backwards stitch by stitch.

On a machine needle the **eye** is just above the point, unlike on a hand sewing needle. This lets the needle carry the top thread under the fabric. There the hook catches the loop and takes it around the bobbin thread. In **lockstitch**, the loop sits in the middle of the fabric. That is why the seam looks the same on both sides.

For normal seams you use straight **lockstitch**. With **zigzag stitch** you sew over the cut edge of the fabric. That way the threads do not fray. This is called **neatening**. At the beginning and end of a seam you sew a few stitches **backwards**. This fastens off the threads, and the seam does not come undone when you wear the garment.

Sometimes **loops** form on the underside of the fabric. Usually the tension of the top thread is then too loose. The bobbin thread then pulls it down. Often the top thread has also been threaded wrongly. Then it helps to take it out completely and thread it again carefully.

In 1830 the French tailor **Barthélemy Thimonnier** received a patent for a sewing machine with chain stitch. He set up a workshop for uniforms. Other tailors feared for their jobs and destroyed his machines. Later, inventors in the USA such as **Isaac Singer** improved the sewing machine. In Switzerland, Karl Friedrich Gegauf founded the company in **Steckborn** in 1893 that became **Bernina**.

gewusst: A modern household sewing machine can sew several hundred stitches a minute.
The first sewing machines were driven by a foot pedal or a hand crank before there were electric motors.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of panorama is a rule in copyright law. It allows you to make pictures of works of art and buildings that stand permanently in public places. So, for example, you may photograph a sculpture in a park and show the photo.
wichtigste: Works of art and buildings are protected by **copyright**.
Freedom of panorama is an exception to this protection.
In Switzerland you may depict works that are permanently on publicly accessible ground.
The depiction must not be three-dimensional.
It must not serve the same purpose as the original.
Other countries have different rules, some of them stricter.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who creates a work of art, a photo or a building is its **author**. **Copyright** protects works like these. Normally only the author may decide who is allowed to copy or depict the work. In Switzerland this protection lasts until 70 years after the author’s death. But there are exceptions, and one of them is **freedom of panorama**.

The Swiss **Copyright Act** says: a work that is permanently on or at publicly accessible ground may be depicted. This includes, for example, **sculptures** in the park, fountains or buildings on the street. You may photograph, film or paint them. You may also show and share the pictures. What matters is that the work stands there **permanently**.

Freedom of panorama has limits. The depiction must **not be three-dimensional**. So you may not rebuild a copy of a sculpture as a figure and sell it. The depiction must also not serve the **same purpose** as the original. In addition, the rule only applies to works that stand there permanently. A short outdoor exhibition does not count.

Every country has its own rules. In **Germany**, freedom of panorama applies mainly to works that can be seen from public streets and squares. In **France** it was very limited for a long time. This is important for projects such as **Wikipedia**, which make many photos freely available. There, for each picture, people have to check which rules apply in the country where the work stands.

gewusst: Whether you may freely use a photo of a building depends on which country the building is in.
The name “freedom of panorama” comes from the idea that you should be free to depict the view over a city or landscape.

teile.einleitung: A self-portrait is a picture that an artist makes of themselves. In the past it was painted with the help of a mirror; today people often take a selfie with their mobile phone.
wichtigste: A portrait shows a person, a self-portrait shows the artist themselves.
In the past you usually needed a mirror.
In a mirror, left and right are swapped.
Albrecht Dürer painted a famous self-portrait in 1500.
Vincent van Gogh painted himself very often.
A selfie is a modern form of self-portrait.

abschnitte.text: A **portrait** is a picture of a person, often only of the head and shoulders. When an artist paints themselves, the result is a **self-portrait**. With it they show what they look like and how they feel. Some artists painted themselves at different ages. That way you can see how they grew older.

To paint himself, a painter in the past needed a **mirror**. In it he sees his face and can copy it. But in a mirror **left and right are swapped**. That is why many self-portraits show a mirrored face. A painter who paints with his right hand sometimes appears in the picture as left-handed.

**Albrecht Dürer** from Nuremberg painted himself from the front, with long curls, in 1500. This picture is especially famous. **Vincent van Gogh** had little money for models and so often painted himself, including with a straw hat. **Rembrandt** and **Frida Kahlo** also created many self-portraits. The Swiss painter **Ferdinand Hodler** often painted himself too.

When you draw a face, you can follow simple **proportions**. The eyes are roughly in the **middle of the head**, not high up as many people think. The ears reach roughly from the eyes to the tip of the nose. With a light guideline, drawing becomes easier. It is best to practise in front of a mirror.

A **selfie** is a photo that you take of yourself with your mobile phone. It is a modern form of self-portrait. Today a huge number of selfies are taken every day. With selfies you should think carefully about which pictures you share on the internet.

gewusst: Van Gogh painted more than 30 self-portraits in just a few years.
In 2013 a large English dictionary chose the English word “selfie” as its word of the year.

teile.einleitung: “Battleship Potemkin” is a Soviet silent film by Sergei Eisenstein from 1925. It tells the story of a sailors’ uprising in 1905 and is seen as one of the most important films in the history of cinema.
wichtigste: The film dates from 1925 and was directed by Sergei Eisenstein.
It is a black-and-white silent film.
It tells the story of a mutiny on a Russian warship in 1905.
The most famous scene takes place on the Odessa Steps.
Eisenstein used montage deliberately to heighten feelings.
Many later films have imitated the steps scene.

abschnitte.text: The film is set in 1905 on the Russian warship Potemkin. The sailors are supposed to eat soup made from rotten meat and refuse. This leads to a **mutiny**, that is, an uprising against the officers. The ship then sails into the port of **Odessa**, where the people side with the sailors. The film is based on a real event, but tells it freely and with a clear political message.

The best-known scene shows a large flight of steps in Odessa. Soldiers march down, and the people on the steps flee in panic. Eisenstein shows the soldiers, the crowd and individual people one after another, including a pram rolling down the steps. The scene is invented; it did not really happen like this. Even so, it became one of the best-known images in film history.

**Montage** means putting individual film shots together. Eisenstein was convinced that a film’s effect comes mainly from the editing. Short shots, hard cuts and a fast **rhythm** are meant to stir up the viewers. Two pictures one after another can in this way create a new meaning that neither has on its own. These ideas are still taught at film schools today.

In the Soviet Union the film was meant as **propaganda** for the revolution. For this reason it was banned or cut for a time in some countries. Film experts, however, value it above all for its visual language. Many directors have later quoted the steps scene, for example with a rolling pram in action films. In polls of experts the film keeps appearing among the best films of all time.

gewusst: Because of the film, the steps in Odessa are now called the Potemkin Stairs.
Eisenstein was only about 27 years old when he made the film.

teile.einleitung: The Merzbau was a work of art you could walk into, which Kurt Schwitters built in his house in Hanover. Over many years he turned rooms into a huge sculpture made of wood, plaster and found objects. The original was destroyed in the Second World War.
wichtigste: Kurt Schwitters lived from 1887 to 1948 and was a German artist.
From the 1920s he built the **Merzbau** in his house in Hanover.
He used wood, plaster and found objects.
The Merzbau is seen as a forerunner of **installation art**.
The original was destroyed in an air raid in the Second World War.
You can visit a reconstruction in the Sprengel Museum in Hanover.

abschnitte.text: Kurt Schwitters glued scraps of paper, tickets and rubbish together into **collages**. On one of his pictures, only the piece “Merz” was left of the word “Commerzbank”. After that he used this name for all his art. Schwitters was close to the art movement **Dada**, which questioned the rules and habits of art. He also wrote poems and sound poems.

In his house in Hanover, Schwitters began to rebuild a room. He added wooden panels, plaster shapes, corners, niches and caves. In them he hid small found objects and keepsakes. Over time the **Merzbau** spread into several rooms. This created a sculpture that you could go inside.

Schwitters had to leave Germany in 1937 because the Nazis rejected his art. He fled to Norway and later to England. In both places he began new buildings of this kind, but they remained unfinished. The Merzbau in Hanover was destroyed in an **air raid** in 1943. Only a few photos of it remain.

The Merzbau is seen as one of the forerunners of **installation art**. This is art that shapes a whole room and that you can walk into. A **reconstruction** was built using the old photos. It is now in the Sprengel Museum in Hanover. In this way visitors can experience roughly what the Merzbau looked like.

gewusst: The name “Merz” came about by chance from a cut-out piece of the word “Commerzbank”.
The reconstruction in the Sprengel Museum was built from the few surviving black-and-white photos.

teile.einleitung: New Music is the name for modern art music from about 1900 onwards that deliberately tries out new sounds and rules. Composers broke with the old habits of major and minor and invented completely new techniques. Some of it sounds unfamiliar at first, but you can hear many ideas from New Music in film music and pop music today.
wichtigste: New Music means the experimental art music since about 1900.
Stravinsky's ballet “The Rite of Spring” caused a scandal in Paris in 1913.
Arnold Schoenberg developed the twelve-tone technique in the early 1920s.
Pierre Schaeffer founded musique concrète in Paris in 1948.
John Cage's work 4′33″ from 1952 consists of the performers' silence.
Steve Reich and Philip Glass represent minimal music.
The Swiss composer Arthur Honegger imitated a steam locomotive in “Pacific 231”.

abschnitte.text: Around 1900 many composers were looking for new sounds. The Frenchman Claude **Debussy** used the whole-tone scale in his piano piece “Voiles”: a symmetrical scale with only six notes per octave, which sounds floating and mysterious. Igor Stravinsky wrote the ballet “The Rite of Spring” with wild rhythms and harsh sounds. At the premiere in Paris in 1913 there was a **scandal**: the audience laughed, whistled and argued loudly.

In the early 1920s Arnold Schoenberg from Vienna developed the **twelve-tone technique**. In it all twelve notes of the octave are equally important and are arranged in a fixed row. After the Second World War composers such as Pierre Boulez and Karlheinz Stockhausen applied this row principle to note length, volume and tone colour as well. This technique is called **serialism**.

In 1948 Pierre Schaeffer founded **musique concrète** in Paris. He recorded everyday noises such as railways on tape and put them together into music. Soon electronic music from the studio appeared too. The American John Cage asked what music actually is: in his piece **4′33″** from 1952 the musicians play nothing for four minutes and 33 seconds, and the audience hears the noises in the hall.

In the 1960s **minimal music** developed in the USA. Its best-known representatives are Steve Reich, Philip Glass and Terry Riley. Typical are short patterns that are repeated very often and changed only slowly. This music has an almost hypnotic effect and later strongly influenced film and pop music.

The Swiss composer **Arthur Honegger**, born in Le Havre in France, wrote the orchestral piece “Pacific 231” in 1923, which imitates a moving steam locomotive. The Basel conductor and patron **Paul Sacher** commissioned new works from many composers, for example Béla Bartók and Stravinsky. Today the Paul Sacher Foundation in Basel collects manuscripts by many composers of the 20th century. The Swiss oboist and composer Heinz Holliger is also known internationally.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scale made only of whole-tone steps, with six notes per octave.
A method of composing in which all twelve notes are used in a fixed row.
Music made from recorded everyday noises.
Music made of short patterns that are repeated often and change slowly.

gewusst: The piece 4′33″ has three movements, even though no notes at all are played in it.
A performance of Cage's organ piece “Organ²/ASLSP” in Halberstadt is meant to last 639 years and will not end until the year 2640.
Arthur Honegger was a great railway fan and said himself that he loved locomotives passionately.

teile.einleitung: Mixed colours are made when you mix two primary colours together. Yellow and blue make green, red and yellow make orange, red and blue make violet. With white, black and water you can make any colour lighter or darker.
wichtigste: The three primary colours in painting are red, yellow and blue.
Colours made from two primary colours are called **mixed colours**: green, orange and violet.
White makes a colour lighter, black makes it darker.
Black and white together make grey.
If you mix all three primary colours, you usually get a dark brown.
For light colours, you start with the light colour and add a little of the dark one.

abschnitte.text: In painting there are three **primary colours**: red, yellow and blue. You can mix many other colours from them. Yellow and blue make **green**. Red and yellow make **orange**. Red and blue make **violet**. These colours are called **mixed colours**.

It depends on how much of each colour you use. If you mix a lot of yellow and only a little blue, you get a light **yellow-green**. With more blue, the green becomes darker and bluer. If you want to mix a light colour, you start with the **light colour**. You add the dark colour only in small amounts, otherwise you need a lot of paint.

**White** lightens any colour. Blue and a lot of white make light blue, almost like the sky. **Black** makes colours darker. Even a little black turns red into dark red. Black and white together make **grey**. The more white there is in it, the lighter the grey becomes.

With **watercolours**, water also plays a part. If you add a lot of water, the colour becomes lighter and paler. The white paper then shows through. If you mix all three primary colours together, the colour becomes dark and brownish. That is why it is worth rinsing your brush well in the water from time to time.

In the **colour wheel**, the primary colours and the mixed colours are arranged in a circle. This makes it easy to see which colours belong together. Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel are called **complementary colours**, for example red and green. A well-known colour wheel was developed by the Swiss artist **Johannes Itten**, who taught at the Bauhaus.

gewusst: Coloured light follows different rules: red, green and blue light together make white.
A screen produces all its colours from tiny red, green and blue dots of light.

teile.einleitung: A repoussoir is a figure or object at the front edge of a picture that leads the eye into the depth of the picture. It is often dark and cut off by the edge of the picture. Painters and photographers use this device to make a picture look more three-dimensional.
wichtigste: A repoussoir stands in the foreground at the edge of the picture.
It is often dark and cut off by the edge.
The name is French and means something like “something that pushes back”.
Through the contrast, the space behind it looks deeper.
Typical repoussoirs are trees, rocks, curtains or figures.

abschnitte.text: The word **repoussoir** comes from the French verb repousser, “to push back”. It means a part of the picture in the **foreground** that visually pushes the rest of the picture backwards. It is often a dark tree, a rock, a curtain or a person who is **cut off** by the edge of the picture. Because this part looks near and dark, the bright landscape behind it seems further away.

Our eye compares what is near and what is far. A dark, large object at the front forms a strong **contrast** with the bright background. This creates a kind of frame through which you look into the picture. This device was especially popular in 17th-century landscape painting. Photographers still use it today, for example when they photograph a landscape through branches or an archway.

gewusst: You can easily try out a repoussoir yourself: a branch at the edge of the picture instantly makes a holiday photo look deeper.

teile.einleitung: Scissors are a tool with two blades that move past each other. In this way they cut paper, fabric or hair. If you know a few simple rules, you can cut neatly and safely.
wichtigste: Ordinary scissors have two blades that cross at a pivot.
You carry scissors closed and with the point facing down.
You pass scissors on handle first.
Fabric scissors are only used for fabric, because paper makes them blunt.
On curves you turn the paper, not the scissors.
Pinking shears cut a zigzag edge.

abschnitte.text: Scissors have two **blades** joined by a screw or rivet. This **pivot** makes the scissors a double lever. When you squeeze the handles together, the sharp edges slide past each other. The material between them is cut through. The closer to the pivot you cut, the more force you have.

You always carry scissors **closed** and with the point facing down. That way, if you trip, you will not hurt anyone. If you want to pass them on, you hold them by the closed blades and hold the **handle** out to the other person. For children there are **craft scissors** with rounded points. After use you put the scissors down closed.

You cut with long, steady cuts, opening the scissors wide as you do so. On a **curve** you keep the scissors still and slowly turn the paper with your other hand. For fine corners you use the tips of the blades. Left-handed people cut more easily with **left-handed scissors**, in which the blades are arranged the other way round. That way they can see the cutting line better.

**Fabric scissors** are big and very sharp. You do not cut paper with them, because paper contains tiny hard particles that make the blades **blunt**. **Pinking shears** have jagged blades and cut a zigzag edge so that the fabric frays less. There are also nail scissors, hairdressing scissors, garden shears and kitchen scissors for all kinds of different jobs.

gewusst: The ancient Romans already used scissors with a pivot in the middle.
Before scissors like these, there were spring shears, in which the two blades were joined by a springy bow, similar to sheep shears today.

teile.einleitung: A portrait is a picture that shows a particular person. It can be painted, drawn, photographed or made as a sculpture. Depending on how much is shown and which way the person is looking, there are different kinds of portraits.
wichtigste: A portrait, also called a likeness, shows a particular person.
A portrait from the side is called a profile.
A bust portrait shows the head, shoulders and chest; a full-length portrait the whole body.
Rembrandt’s “Night Watch” is a group portrait.
If you show yourself, you create a self-portrait.
With photography, portraits became affordable for many people.

abschnitte.text: If the person looks straight ahead, it is called a **frontal view**. In **profile** you see the face exactly from the side. You know side views like this from coins, including Swiss francs. A very common one is the three-quarter view, in which the face is turned slightly to the side. It looks lively and shows the shape of the face well.

A portrait can show different amounts of a person. The **bust portrait** shows the head, shoulders and chest. In a half-length portrait you see the body down to the hips. The **full-length portrait** shows the person from head to toe. The more is shown, the more you learn about clothes, posture and surroundings.

A **group portrait** shows several people in one picture. In the Netherlands in the 17th century, societies and guilds liked to be painted together. A famous example is Rembrandt’s “Night Watch” from 1642. It shows a group of Amsterdam citizens from a militia company who seem to be in motion. The picture now hangs in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

In a **self-portrait** the artist shows themselves, often with the help of a mirror. Rembrandt and the Swiss painter **Ferdinand Hodler** created many self-portraits. In the past only rich people could have themselves painted. With **photography** in the 19th century, portraits became affordable for many. Today the selfie is a very everyday form of self-portrait.

gewusst: Probably the most famous portrait in the world is Leonardo da Vinci’s “Mona Lisa” in the Louvre in Paris.
“The Night Watch” is called that because the varnish made the picture darken; the scene actually takes place during the day.

teile.einleitung: Pipilotti Rist is a Swiss artist who became known above all for videos and room installations. Her works are colourful, playful and often have surprising twists. She is one of the internationally best-known Swiss artists.
wichtigste: Pipilotti Rist was born in 1962 in Grabs in the canton of St Gallen.
She works mainly with video, music and light.
Her artist’s name combines Pippi Longstocking with her nickname Lotti.
The video work “Ever Is Over All” was shown at the Venice Biennale in 1997.
In it, a cheerful woman smashes car windows with a flower.

abschnitte.text: Pipilotti Rist’s real name is Elisabeth Charlotte Rist. She was born in 1962 in **Grabs** in the canton of St Gallen. She formed her artist’s name from **Pippi Longstocking** and her nickname Lotti. She studied in Vienna and Basel, among other places, and also made music in a band. Today she lives and works in Zurich.

In the **video work** “Ever Is Over All”, a young woman walks cheerfully along a street. As she goes, she smashes the windows of parked cars with a long flower. A policewoman comes by and greets her in a friendly way. The cheerful music does not fit the destructive action at all, and it is exactly this **contrast** that makes the work exciting. In 1997 it was shown at the **Venice Biennale** and made Rist famous worldwide.

Rist often projects her videos onto the walls, ceilings or floors of whole rooms. Visitors can lie down and immerse themselves in colours, sounds and images. Works like this are called **installations**. Common themes are the body, nature and the joy of colour. In 2009 she also made a feature film, “Pepperminta”.

gewusst: For “Ever Is Over All”, Pipilotti Rist won a prize for young artists at the Venice Biennale in 1997.

teile.einleitung: A nail is a pointed pin used to join pieces of wood. You knock it into the wood with a hammer. Nails are among the oldest and simplest ways of joining things.
wichtigste: Nails are usually made of **steel**, that is, metal.
A nail has a flat **head** at the top, a long shank and a point at the bottom.
You strike the head of the nail with the hammer.
At the start you hold the nail with your fingers and only tap lightly.
Too close to the edge, the wood can split when you nail it.
You pull nails out again with pincers or the claw of the hammer.

abschnitte.text: A nail has three parts. At the top is the flat **head**, which you strike with the hammer. In the middle is the long **shank**. At the bottom is the **point**, which goes into the wood. Most nails are made of **steel**. That is why they are hard enough to go into wood without bending.

At the start you hold the nail firmly between **thumb and index finger**. Then you tap the head very lightly with the hammer. As soon as the nail is firmly in the wood, you take your fingers away. Now you can strike harder. You hold the hammer at the end of the handle and strike straight so that the nail does not bend.

A nail pushes the **wood fibres** apart. If there is too little wood at the edge, the board splits open. We say the wood **splits**. That is why you do not knock nails in too close to the edge. With hard wood or narrow strips you can drill a small hole first. This is called **pre-drilling**.

There are nails in many sizes and shapes. Small, thin nails are also called **panel pins**. There are nails with a wide head for roofing felt and nails with a small head that you can hardly see in the wood. In the past nails were made one by one by hand by blacksmiths. Today machines make them from wire in large quantities.

gewusst: The ancient Romans already used iron nails.
Today nail guns that shoot nails into wood with compressed air are often used on building sites.

teile.einleitung: Surrealism is an art movement that began in Paris in the 1920s. The artists wanted to make dreams, fantasies and the unconscious visible, that is, what lies behind normal reality. That is why you often see strange things in Surrealist pictures, such as melting clocks or floating stones.
wichtigste: Surrealism began in 1924 with André Breton’s “Surrealist Manifesto”.
The word means roughly “above reality”.
The Surrealists were inspired by dreams and by the ideas of Sigmund Freud.
In 1931 Salvador Dalí painted the melting clocks of “The Persistence of Memory”.
René Magritte painted a pipe and wrote underneath it that it was not a pipe.
The Surrealists invented techniques such as frottage and games such as cadavre exquis.
The Swiss artists Meret Oppenheim and Alberto Giacometti also belonged to the movement.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the French “sur” for “above” and “réalisme” for realism. The term “surrealist” was first used by the poet Guillaume Apollinaire in 1917. In 1924 **André Breton** published the first **“Surrealist Manifesto”** in Paris. In it he described art as a way to the **unconscious**, that is, to thoughts that we do not consciously control.

With his book “The Interpretation of Dreams”, the Viennese doctor **Sigmund Freud** had shown that dreams reveal a lot about a person. The Surrealists found this idea exciting. They painted dream pictures in which things are in the wrong places or change into something else. A forerunner was the **Dada** movement, which began at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in 1916.

In **automatic writing** (écriture automatique) you write very fast, without thinking, whatever comes into your head. In 1925 **Max Ernst** developed **frottage**, in which you rub textures such as wood grain onto paper with a pencil. In the game **cadavre exquis**, several people add to a sentence or figure one after another without seeing what came before. This produces funny and surprising results that you can easily try out at school too.

In 1931 the Spaniard **Salvador Dalí** painted “The Persistence of Memory” with soft, melting pocket watches. The small picture now hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The Belgian **René Magritte** painted a pipe with the inscription “Ceci n’est pas une pipe”, that is, “This is not a pipe”. With it he wanted to show that a picture is only an image and not the object itself. Films were also part of Surrealism, for example “Un Chien Andalou” (An Andalusian Dog) by Luis Buñuel and Dalí from 1929.

In 1936 the artist **Meret Oppenheim** covered a cup, a saucer and a spoon with fur. The object “Breakfast in Fur” became world-famous. The sculptor **Alberto Giacometti** from the Grisons belonged to the Paris Surrealists from about 1930 to 1935. His sculpture “The Palace at 4 a.m.” dates from this time.

Surrealism influenced painting, literature, photography and film. To this day advertising, music videos and fantasy films use Surrealist ideas. When we call something “surreal” in everyday life, we mean that it seems strange, as if in a dream.

begriffe.erklaerung: A public statement in which a group describes its aims and ideas.
Thoughts and feelings inside us that we are not consciously aware of.
A technique in which you rub over a surface with a pencil onto paper.
A game in which several people put together a picture or sentence without seeing the others’ parts.

gewusst: Meret Oppenheim was only about 22 years old when she made the fur cup.
Salvador Dalí was famous for his long moustache twirled upwards.
The game cadavre exquis means “exquisite corpse”, after the first sentence it produced.

teile.einleitung: In a series circuit, several devices are connected one after another on a single path for the current. The current has to flow through all of them in turn. If one part fails, the whole circuit is broken.
wichtigste: In a series circuit there is only one single path for the current.
If one lamp breaks, all the others go out too.
The same current flows through all the devices.
The voltage is shared among the devices.
Batteries in series together give a higher voltage.

abschnitte.text: In a **series circuit**, the devices are lined up like beads on a string. The current flows from the source through the first lamp, then through the second and back again. There is no branch. If the circuit is broken at one point, for example because the filament of a lamp snaps, no **current** flows anywhere any more. All the lamps go out.

In a series circuit the **current** is the same at every point. The **voltage** of the source, on the other hand, is shared among the individual devices. That is why two identical lamps on one battery shine more weakly than a single one. The **resistances** also add up: the more devices, the greater the total resistance.

In many torches the batteries lie one behind the other. Two 1.5-volt batteries in series give 3 volts together. A **switch** is also always in series with the device it switches on and off. In the past many fairy lights were connected in series, which is why the whole string went out when one little bulb was faulty. The opposite is the **parallel circuit**.

gewusst: With fairy lights in series, people often used to have to check every little bulb one by one to find the faulty one.

teile.einleitung: Pop music is music made for a wide audience that is liked by many people. The word “pop” comes from “popular”, meaning well liked and well known. Pop songs are usually short, have a catchy melody and a chorus that you can quickly sing along to.
wichtigste: The name “pop” is derived from the word popular.
A chorus that comes back the same way several times is typical of pop songs.
Michael Jackson was called the “King of Pop”.
The first Eurovision Song Contest took place in Lugano in 1956.
Nemo won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 2024.
That is why the contest took place in Basel in 2025.
The best-known music award in the USA is the Grammy.

abschnitte.text: Pop music developed in the 1950s and 1960s from rock 'n' roll, Schlager, soul and other styles. A typical pop song lasts about three to four minutes and consists of **verse**, chorus and often a bridge. The **chorus** comes back the same way several times and sticks in your head particularly well. Pop is spread by record companies, radio, music videos and today above all by streaming.

The Beatles from Liverpool were among the first worldwide pop stars in the 1960s. **Michael Jackson** was called the “King of Pop”; his album “Thriller” from 1982 is regarded as one of the best-selling albums of all time. Madonna was given the nickname “Queen of Pop”. Today artists such as Taylor Swift, Beyoncé and Ed Sheeran are among the most successful pop stars in the world.

The **Eurovision Song Contest** is a big singing competition in which countries from Europe and a few others compete against each other. The first contest took place in 1956 in **Lugano**, and the Swiss singer Lys Assia won with the song “Refrain”. In 1988 Céline Dion won for Switzerland. In 2024 **Nemo** from Biel won with the song “The Code”, which is why the contest took place in Basel in 2025.

The **charts**, also called the hit parade, show how successful a song is. They count sales, downloads and streams. Switzerland has had an official hit parade since 1968. The most important music award in the USA is the **Grammy**, which has been presented since 1959; in Switzerland there are the Swiss Music Awards.

Today most people listen to pop music via **streaming** on their mobile phones. Songs often become known through social media and short videos, sometimes all over the world within a few days. Many pop songs are written jointly by several songwriters and producers. K-pop from South Korea is also a pop music with fans all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of a song that comes back several times with the same words.
A ranking of the currently most successful songs.
Playing music directly from the internet without buying it.
A person who writes songs, that is the melody and the words.

gewusst: Switzerland won the very first Eurovision Song Contest in 1956 and also the contest in 2024.
Céline Dion comes from Canada but sang for Switzerland in 1988 and won.
Michael Jackson's “moonwalk” became one of the most famous dance steps in pop history.

teile.einleitung: Musical notation is a system of signs with which you can write music down. With it you can record exactly which notes are played, for how long and how loudly. Thanks to musical notation, musicians all over the world can play pieces that were composed hundreds of years ago.
wichtigste: Notes are written on a staff of five lines.
The treble clef is also called the G clef.
A whole note (semibreve) lasts as long as four quarter notes (crotchets).
A half note (minim) lasts as long as four eighth notes (quavers).
A dot to the right of a note lengthens it by half.
The sharp raises a note by a semitone.
The note called “B” in English is called H in German-speaking countries.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages monks wrote small signs above the words of songs, called **neumes**. They only showed roughly whether the melody went up or down. In the 11th century Guido of Arezzo suggested using lines so that you could read the exact pitch. From this, step by step, today's notation with five lines developed, and since the 17th century it has looked largely as it does today.

Notes sit on and between the five lines of the **staff** (stave). Right at the front is a clef, which determines which note is on which line. The **treble clef** or G clef curls around the second line, where g¹ lies, and is used for high instruments. For low instruments such as the cello or tuba the bass clef is used, also called the F clef. Very high or low notes are written on small ledger lines.

The shape of a note shows how long it lasts. A **whole note** (semibreve) is an empty circle without a stem, a half note (minim) has a stem, a quarter note (crotchet) is filled in, and an eighth note (quaver) also has a little flag. A whole note lasts as long as two half notes or four quarter notes, and a half note as long as four eighth notes. A **dot** to the right of the note lengthens it by half its value. For places where nobody plays there are rest signs.

With **accidentals** you change the pitch. The **sharp** (♯) raises a note by a semitone, so C becomes C sharp. The flat (♭) lowers a note by a semitone, so E becomes E flat. The natural sign cancels an accidental. By the way, in German-speaking countries the note after A is called H, and the note B there is H lowered by a semitone, which is B flat in English.

Music contains many other instructions. Time signatures such as 3/4 show how many beats a **bar** has, and bar lines separate the bars. Words such as Allegro give the tempo, and signs such as p and f the volume. Repeat signs show that a section is played again. Besides staff notation there are other ways of writing music, such as guitar fingerings as tablature or chord symbols such as Am and G.

begriffe.erklaerung: The five lines on and between which the notes are written.
A sign at the beginning of the line that sets the pitches of the lines.
Early musical signs of the Middle Ages written above the words of songs.
A sign such as the sharp or flat that raises or lowers a note.
An edition of music in which all the parts of a piece are written one below the other.

gewusst: The fact that the note is called H in German-speaking countries probably goes back to a medieval mix-up between a square-shaped b and the letter h.
There is a musical notation in braille for blind musicians.
The score of a large symphony can have over 30 staves on a single page.

teile.einleitung: A museum is a building in which works of art, old objects or things from nature and technology are collected, kept and exhibited. There you can see dinosaur skeletons, famous paintings, locomotives or suits of armour up close. Switzerland has more than 1,000 museums, more than almost any other country relative to its population.
wichtigste: A museum collects, keeps, researches and shows works of art or objects.
The word comes from the Greek “Mouseion”, a place of the Muses.
The Louvre in Paris is one of the largest and most visited art museums in the world.
In art museums you are usually not allowed to touch the pictures.
The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne shows vehicles, aircraft and ships.
The National Museum in Zurich has the largest collection on Swiss history.
A gallery exhibits pictures and often sells them too.

abschnitte.text: A **museum** is an institution that collects things, keeps them carefully, researches them and shows them to the public. The word comes from the Greek **Mouseion**, a shrine of the Muses, the goddesses of the arts. In ancient times the Mouseion of Alexandria in Egypt, a place for scholars, was famous. There are art museums, natural history museums, history museums, technology museums and many more.

A **curator** chooses which objects are shown and plans exhibitions. **Conservators** carefully clean and repair old pictures and objects. Museum educators explain the exhibitions to children and school classes. Many treasures are kept in the **store**, because there is not enough room for everything in the exhibition rooms.

In art museums you are usually not allowed to touch the pictures, because sweat and grease on your hands damage the paint. That is why there are often barriers and attendants. Flash photography is often banned, because strong light can fade old colours. But many museums also have areas where you can touch things and join in, especially for children.

The **Louvre** in Paris used to be a royal palace and opened as a museum in 1793. It shows the Mona Lisa and is visited by around 9 million people every year, as of about 2024. Other famous museums are the British Museum in London, the Vatican Museums in Rome and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. A **gallery**, on the other hand, exhibits pictures and often sells them too.

The **Swiss Museum of Transport** in Lucerne opened in 1959 and shows locomotives, aircraft, ships and space travel; it is one of the most visited museums in the country. The **National Museum** in Zurich, opened in 1898, has the largest collection on Swiss history. In Bern there is the Zentrum Paul Klee, and in Riehen near Basel the Fondation Beyeler. The Kunstmuseum Basel is seen as the oldest public art collection in the world.

Many museums offer tours for children, puzzle booklets or audio guides. With the **Swiss Museum Pass** you can visit hundreds of museums for a year. Every year in May there is International Museum Day, with special offers. It is worth not trying to see everything at once, but picking out a few favourite pieces.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who plans exhibitions and chooses objects.
An expert who looks after and repairs old works of art and objects.
A museum’s storeroom for objects that are not on show at the moment.
A place where pictures are exhibited and often sold.

gewusst: The public art collection in Basel goes back to 1661, when the city bought a private collection.
There is also a large planetarium at the Museum of Transport in Lucerne.
The glass pyramid in front of the Louvre was opened in 1989 and now serves as the main entrance.

teile.einleitung: Robert Frank was a photographer and film-maker from Zurich. With his photo book “The Americans” he showed the USA as unvarnished as hardly anyone before him. The book is seen as one of the most important photo books of all.
wichtigste: Robert Frank was born in Zurich in 1924 and died in Canada in 2019.
In 1947 he emigrated to the USA.
With a Guggenheim Fellowship he travelled right across the USA.
His book “The Americans” was published in Paris in 1958 and in New York in 1959.
Later he also made films.

abschnitte.text: Robert Frank was born in **Zurich** in 1924. He learned photography in Switzerland from various photographers. In 1947 he emigrated to **New York** and first worked for fashion magazines. But soon he wanted to photograph more freely and show people’s everyday lives. He also travelled to South America and around Europe.

With a **Guggenheim Fellowship**, a grant for artists and researchers, Frank travelled through the USA by car in the mid-1950s. He took thousands of pictures and chose 83 of them for his book **“The Americans”**. It shows petrol stations, jukeboxes, flags, funerals, lonely roads and people who are treated differently. The book was published in Paris in 1958 and in New York in 1959, with a foreword by the writer Jack Kerouac.

At first many people found the pictures too gloomy, crooked or blurred. Frank did not show the shiny image that the USA liked to have of itself, but loneliness and differences between people. It was precisely this that later made the book so famous. It shaped generations of **street photographers**. After that, Frank turned mainly to **film**.

gewusst: For “The Americans”, Robert Frank took more than 20,000 pictures; only 83 went into the book.

teile.einleitung: A switch opens or closes a circuit. When it is closed, current flows and the lamp lights up. In the “off” position a gap appears and the current stops flowing.
wichtigste: A switch opens or closes a circuit.
In the “off” position it breaks the circuit.
A switch is in series with the device it switches.
A push button only switches while you press it.
With a two-way switch circuit you can switch a lamp from two places.

abschnitte.text: Current can only flow in a closed **circuit**. Inside the switch there are two metal contacts. When you press “on”, the contacts touch and the circuit is **closed**. With “off”, the contacts are separated and a gap appears. The circuit is **open**, and the lamp goes out.

A normal **light switch** stays in its position until you press it again. A **push button**, for example on a doorbell, only switches while your finger is on it. In stairwells or long corridors there is often a **two-way switch circuit**. With it you can switch the same lamp on and off with two switches in different places. Some lamps also switch on through motion sensors or via a mobile phone.

Switches are built so that you cannot touch the live parts. **Insulation** made of plastic protects your hand. Even so, you should never touch switches and sockets with wet hands. If a switch is damaged, only a qualified person may repair it.

gewusst: Inside many switches, a small spring makes sure the contacts snap quickly and safely.

teile.einleitung: The hem is the turned-up and stitched edge of a piece of clothing, for example at the bottom of a pair of trousers or a skirt. It stops the fabric fraying and sets the right length. Hemming is one of the first things you learn when sewing.
wichtigste: The hem is the turned-up and stitched edge of a fabric.
It stops the edge of the fabric fraying.
The hem is used to set the right length.
When hemming, you turn the edge over, iron it and sew it down.
A blind stitch can hardly be seen from the outside.

abschnitte.text: A freshly cut edge of fabric **frays** because the threads come loose. When **hemming**, you turn the edge over and sew it down, so it stays neat. At the same time the hem decides how long a pair of trousers, a skirt or a sleeve is. If trousers are too long, you can shorten them and hem them again. Curtains and tablecloths have hems too.

First you measure the length you want and mark it with tailor’s chalk. Then you turn the edge over once narrowly and a second time more widely, so that the raw edge disappears inside. With the **iron** you press the fold flat and pin it in place with **pins**. Then you sew it on by hand or with the sewing machine. The **blind stitch** only catches a few threads of the outer fabric, so you can hardly see it from the outside.

gewusst: In German, the edge of a forest is also called a “Saum”, or “Waldsaum”.

teile.einleitung: In metalwork you shape metal by marking out, sawing, filing, drilling and bending. You need special tools for this, because metal is much harder than wood. In handicraft lessons you learn the most important steps.
wichtigste: Lines on metal are marked with a **scriber**.
A metal tube is cut with a **hacksaw**.
Sharp edges after sawing are removed by **deburring**.
The workpiece is clamped firmly in the vice while you work.
Before drilling, you mark the spot with a centre punch.
Safety glasses protect your eyes from metal shavings.

abschnitte.text: Before you work on metal, you mark the lines. This is called **marking out**. For this you use a **scriber** with a hard point. It scratches a fine, clearly visible line into the surface. A pencil would be too inaccurate on metal. With a steel rule and a square, the lines become straight and at right angles.

To cut tubes, rods and sheets you use the **hacksaw**. It has a finely toothed, hardened blade held tight in a frame. The workpiece is clamped firmly in the **vice** while you do this. Then you bring the edges into the shape you want with the **file**. Files can be coarse or fine, flat, round or triangular.

Sawing and drilling leave small, sharp bits of metal at the edge. They are called **burrs**. They are removed with a file or a deburring tool. This step is called **deburring**. It is important so that you do not cut yourself on the edges and the parts fit together well.

Before drilling, you knock a small dent into the metal with the **centre punch**. That way the drill does not slip. When drilling, the workpiece is held firmly or clamped. Thin sheets and wires can be **bent** with pliers or in the vice. This is how hooks, holders or small figures are made, for example.

In metalwork, small **shavings** often fly about. That is why you wear **safety glasses**. You tie long hair back, especially at the drilling machine. You never brush shavings away with your hand, but with a brush. In the subject of technical design at Swiss schools, you learn these rules right from the start.

gewusst: The teeth of a metal saw blade are much finer than those of a wood saw blade.
When drilling metal, a drop of oil often helps to stop the drill getting too hot.

teile.einleitung: The world format is a paper format that is used in Switzerland mainly for posters. The best-known world format poster measures about 90 by 128 centimetres. You see these posters at stations, on streets and in squares.
wichtigste: The world format was introduced at the beginning of the 20th century.
The F4 poster format measures about 90 by 128 centimetres.
In Switzerland it is still the standard for poster hoardings today.
It does not match the A paper sizes you know from writing paper.
As with the A sizes, the long side is about 1.41 times as long as the short side.

abschnitte.text: The **world format** is a system of paper sizes that was introduced around 1913. As with the **A paper sizes**, every sheet has the same ratio of sides. If you cut a sheet in half, you get another sheet with the same proportions. But the sizes are different from the A sizes. That is why a world format poster does not exactly match an A size.

In Switzerland the **F4** format, about 90 by 128 centimetres, is the classic poster format. Originally it measured 90.5 by 128 centimetres, today usually 89.5 by 128 centimetres. Many posters of this size hang on the **poster hoardings** at stations and along streets. Advertising, concerts and votes are announced with them. Switzerland is internationally known for its **poster art**, and many graphic designers create work for this format.

gewusst: In many other countries the world format is hardly known, but in Switzerland it still shapes the look of the streets today.

teile.einleitung: In knitting, a single thread is turned into a fabric made of many loops called stitches. With two needles and some wool you can make scarves, hats and socks.
wichtigste: The two basic stitches are knit and purl.
Stocking stitch is made of knit rows on the front and purl rows on the back.
Garter stitch is made by knitting all rows.
Socks are traditionally knitted in the round on a set of double-pointed needles.
At the end the work is cast off.
Knitting is stretchy because it is made of loops.

abschnitte.text: A piece of knitting consists of **stitches**, that is, loops that hang into each other. First you cast the stitches on to a needle. Then you knit row by row. There are two basic stitches: **knit** and **purl**. Almost all patterns are made of these two. A knit stitch looks like a purl stitch on the back.

If you knit on the right-side rows and purl on the wrong-side rows, you get **stocking stitch**. On the front you see small V-shaped stitches, on the back only purl stitches. If, on the other hand, you knit every row, you get **garter stitch**. Then you see horizontal ridges on both sides. Garter stitch does not curl at the edge and is good for your first scarf.

Socks, hats and gloves are often knitted **in the round**, without a seam. Traditionally you need a **set of double-pointed needles** for this. It usually consists of five short needles with points at both ends. The stitches are spread over four needles and you knit with the fifth. Today there are also circular needles with a cable between them.

When the piece of knitting is long enough, it is **cast off**. You pull each stitch over the next one until only one loop is left. Then you pull the thread through and **weave it in**. Knitted fabric is stretchy because the loops can change shape and move. In a woven fabric, on the other hand, straight threads cross that hardly give at all.

gewusst: Many jumpers, T-shirts and socks are made by knitting machines today.
With urban knitting, knitting even becomes street art in public spaces.

teile.einleitung: A sculpture is a three-dimensional figure that an artist makes out of stone, wood, metal, clay or other materials. Unlike a picture, you can look at a sculpture from all sides and sometimes even walk around it. Artists who make sculptures are called sculptors.
wichtigste: A sculpture is a figure made of stone, wood, metal or other materials.
Someone who makes sculptures is called a sculptor.
With stone you work with a hammer and chisel.
Clay figures are fired in a kiln after they have been shaped.
Bronze figures are made by pouring liquid metal.
Alberto Giacometti and Jean Tinguely are famous Swiss sculptors.
The Statue of Liberty in New York is one of the best-known sculptures in the world.

abschnitte.text: A **sculpture** is a work of art with height, width and depth. People also speak of **plastic art** or sculpting. If a figure is only half carved out of a surface, it is called a **relief**. There are sculptures in museums, in squares, in parks and on churches.

With stone and wood, the sculptor takes material away. With a **hammer and chisel** he knocks off piece after piece until the figure appears. With clay or wax, you add material and shape it with your hands. Figures made of **clay** then become hard in the kiln. For bronze figures you make a mould and pour liquid metal into it; this is called **casting**.

One of the oldest figures is the Venus of Willendorf, which is around 30,000 years old and only about eleven centimetres tall. The ancient Greeks made lifelike statues of marble. In the Renaissance, **Michelangelo** carved the David, more than five metres tall, out of marble. Around 1880 the Frenchman **Auguste Rodin** created the thoughtful seated figure “The Thinker”.

The **Statue of Liberty** stands on an island off New York and holds up a torch. France gave it to the USA, and it was unveiled in 1886. The figure itself is about 46 metres tall; with the pedestal it is around 93 metres. Its outer skin is made of thin copper plates that have turned green with verdigris.

**Alberto Giacometti** came from the Bregaglia valley in the Grisons. He became famous for very thin, long bronze figures, for example the “Walking Man”. His picture was on the former Swiss 100-franc note. **Jean Tinguely** from Fribourg built moving machines out of scrap that rattle and make a noise. His Carnival Fountain and the Museum Tinguely are in Basel.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artist who makes figures out of stone, wood, metal or clay.
A tool with a sharp edge used to knock pieces off stone.
A figure that only partly sticks out from a flat wall or panel.
A metal made of copper and tin that is easy to cast.

gewusst: There used to be a platform in the torch of the Statue of Liberty that visitors could climb up to.
A Giacometti figure is one of the most expensive sculptures ever sold at auction.
Rodin’s Thinker exists in many bronze casts that stand in museums all over the world.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Style is a Swiss style of graphic design from the 1950s and 1960s. Internationally it became known as the International Typographic Style. It still shapes posters, books and logos today.
wichtigste: The Swiss Style began in the 1950s and 1960s.
Internationally it is called the International Typographic Style.
Typical features are design grids and sans serif typefaces.
Texts are often set ranged left and ragged right.
Its centres were Zurich and Basel.
The typefaces Helvetica and Univers were created in this period.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss Style relies on **clarity**. Designers arrange text and pictures on an invisible **design grid**. This makes everything look orderly and calm. Instead of drawings, **objective photography** is often used. Decorations are left out so that the message comes first.

Typical are **sans serif typefaces**, that is, typefaces without little feet. The text is usually **ranged left and ragged right**: on the left all lines start at the same point, on the right they end at different points. In 1957 two famous typefaces appeared: **Helvetica** from Münchenstein near Basel and **Univers** by the Swiss Adrian Frutiger. Both are still used all over the world today.

The centres of the style were **Zurich** and **Basel**, above all their schools of design. In Zurich the graphic designer **Josef Müller-Brockmann** worked; he is known for his concert posters. In Basel **Armin Hofmann** and **Emil Ruder** taught. Many students from all over the world came to Switzerland to learn there. In this way the style spread internationally.

The style became a model for company logos, road signs and signposts at airports. Many websites and apps also follow its principles. Clear grids and readable typefaces help people understand information quickly. That is why the Swiss Style is seen as one of the most influential graphic styles of the 20th century.

gewusst: The typeface Helvetica was first called Neue Haas Grotesk and was later renamed after the Latin name for Switzerland.
A whole documentary film has even been made about Helvetica.

teile.einleitung: A rivet joins two or more parts, usually of sheet metal or metal, firmly together. To do this you push it through a hole and deform it so that it can no longer slip out. A riveted joint cannot simply be undone again.
wichtigste: Rivets join sheets and other parts permanently.
A riveted joint is **permanent**: you have to destroy the rivet to open it.
A **blind rivet** can be used when you can only reach one side.
Blind rivets are also called pop rivets and are set with a rivet gun.
The Eiffel Tower is held together by a great many rivets.
Jeans also have small rivets on the pockets.

abschnitte.text: A classic rivet has a head and a shank, rather like a nail without a point. You push it through a hole in the parts that are to be joined. Then the other end is pressed flat with a hammer or a machine. This creates a second head, the **closing head**. The parts are pressed tightly together between the two heads.

Sometimes you can only reach the workpiece from one side, for example with a tube or a box. Then you use a **blind rivet**, also called a **pop rivet**. Inside it is a thin metal pin, the **mandrel**. With a rivet gun you pull the mandrel out. As you do so, the rivet is squeezed together at the back and becomes wider until it holds.

In the past, large steel structures were almost always riveted. The **Eiffel Tower** in Paris is held together by around 2.5 million rivets. Many old **railway bridges**, ships and steam boilers are also riveted. Today steel parts are often welded or bolted. In **aircraft construction**, however, rivets are still very important, because they are light and reliable.

You also find rivets on many small things. On **jeans** they strengthen the corners of the pockets. On bags, belts and shoes they hold parts together or serve as decoration. Scissors and pliers also often have a rivet as a pivot. In handicraft lessons you can build simple sheet metal boxes with blind rivets.

gewusst: When large steel bridges were built, the rivets used to be put in red-hot; as they cooled they shrank and pressed the parts together even more tightly.
The rivets on jeans were patented in 1873.

teile.einleitung: With perspective you can show depth and space on a flat sheet. Things in the distance are drawn smaller, and lines meet at one point. This technique was carefully researched in Florence about 600 years ago.
wichtigste: Parallel lines leading into the distance meet at the vanishing point.
The horizon is always at the viewer’s eye level.
One-point perspective has one vanishing point, two-point perspective two, three-point perspective three.
Around 1420 Filippo Brunelleschi showed experiments on one-point perspective in Florence.
Worm’s-eye view means looking from below, bird’s-eye view looking from above.
Distant things look smaller and often paler.

abschnitte.text: If you look along a long, straight road, its edges seem to come together in the distance. The point where they meet is called the **vanishing point**. It lies on the **horizon line**, which shows the viewer’s eye level. If you climb a ladder, the horizon in the picture moves up and you see more of the ground. If you bend down, it sinks.

abschnitte.titel: One, two or three vanishing points
abschnitte.text: In **one-point perspective** you look straight into a room or along a street, and all the lines going into the distance run to one point. If you draw a house from its corner, you see two sides. This is **two-point perspective**, with two vanishing points on the horizon. With very tall buildings seen at an angle from below, the vertical edges also come together. Then you need a third vanishing point above or below; this is **three-point perspective**.

In a **worm’s-eye view**, sometimes called frog’s-eye view, you look up from the ground. People and buildings then look huge and powerful. In a **bird’s-eye view** you look down from high above on a city or landscape, just as a bird does in flight. You get a good overview, and everything looks smaller. Photographers and film-makers use both angles to create a particular mood.

In the Middle Ages, important figures were often simply painted bigger than others, without real space. In the **Renaissance**, artists wanted to show the world as the eye sees it. Around 1420 the Florentine architect **Filippo Brunelleschi** used mirrors to demonstrate how to show buildings in correct perspective. He also built the famous dome of Florence Cathedral. Shortly afterwards **Leon Battista Alberti** wrote down the rules of one-point perspective in a book about painting.

As well as lines, there is also **aerial perspective**. Mountains and forests in the distance appear lighter, paler and slightly bluish, because the air in between changes the light. Painters make use of this by painting distant things in cooler, lighter colours. Overlapping also helps: what is in front hides what lies behind it.

gewusst: Leonardo da Vinci studied aerial perspective closely and described how colours fade in the distance.
Computer games also calculate their 3D worlds according to the rules of perspective.

teile.einleitung: William Henry Fox Talbot was an English researcher and one of the inventors of photography. He developed a process in which a negative is made first. From it you could make as many prints as you liked, and this shaped photography for more than 150 years.
wichtigste: Talbot lived in England from 1800 to 1877.
He invented the negative-positive process in photography.
His process was called the calotype, also known as the talbotype.
Many prints could be made from one paper negative.
A daguerreotype, on the other hand, was always one of a kind.

abschnitte.text: Talbot was a **mathematician**, language scholar and inventor. He lived on the country estate of **Lacock Abbey** in southern England. Because he was not good at drawing, he looked for a way to capture pictures with light. He soaked paper in light-sensitive **silver salts** and put it in a camera. An early negative from 1835 shows a window of his house; it is one of the oldest surviving negatives in the world.

In Talbot’s process, a **negative** is made first: what is light is dark and what is dark is light. If you lay this paper negative on a second sheet of light-sensitive paper and expose it, a **positive** is made. You can repeat this as often as you like. In 1841 Talbot patented this process as the **calotype**. The word comes from Greek and means something like “beautiful picture”.

Almost at the same time, in 1839, Louis Daguerre in France presented the **daguerreotype**. It showed very sharp pictures on a metal plate, but was always **one of a kind**. Talbot’s pictures were a little less sharp, but they could be copied. Later Talbot published the book “The Pencil of Nature”, one of the first books with photographs. The principle of negative and print remained usual until digital photography.

gewusst: The title “The Pencil of Nature” refers to light drawing pictures like a pencil.
Talbot discovered that a barely visible picture on the paper could be brought out with chemicals, so the exposure time could be much shorter.

teile.einleitung: A **clef** stands at the beginning of every line of music and determines which note is on which line. Without a clef you would not know how high a note sounds. The most important ones are the treble clef, the bass clef and the C clefs.
wichtigste: The treble clef is also called the G clef, the bass clef the F clef.
In the treble clef the lines from the bottom are e¹, g¹, b¹, d² and f².
In the lowest space of the treble clef is f¹.
In the bass clef the bottom line is great G, the top line small a.
The cello is usually written in the bass clef.
The alto and tenor clefs are C clefs.

abschnitte.text: The clefs developed from letters. The **treble clef** is a decorated G; its curl circles the second line and shows **g¹** there. The **bass clef** is a reshaped F; its two dots lie around the fourth line, on which small f stands. The **C clefs** point with their middle to **c¹** (middle C).

In the **treble clef** the five lines from bottom to top carry the notes **e¹, g¹, b¹, d²** and **f²**. So the middle line is b¹. In the spaces are **f¹, a¹, c²** and **e²**. It is used for high instruments such as the violin, flute and trumpet and for the right hand on the piano.

The **bass clef** is meant for low notes. On its lines, from the bottom, are **great G**, great B, small d, small f and small **a**. Instruments that play in the bass clef include the **cello**, double bass, bassoon, trombone and tuba. On the piano the left hand usually reads in the bass clef.

The **C clefs** can sit on different lines. In the **alto clef** the middle points to the third line, and that is where c¹ is. It is used mainly by the **viola**. In the **tenor clef** c¹ is on the fourth line. The cello, bassoon and trombone sometimes switch to the tenor clef in high registers so that not too many ledger lines are needed.
