Many people learn the notes with **memory sentences** or by counting from a line they know. In the treble clef the second line with g¹ is a good starting point. On the piano c¹ lies exactly between the treble and bass clefs. In both it sits on a ledger line, once below and once above.

gewusst: In the past there were even more clefs, such as the soprano clef, which is hardly used today.
The viola is one of the few instruments that are almost always written in the alto clef.

teile.einleitung: Almost every note we hear is made up of many partials. Above the fundamental, quieter, higher notes vibrate along with it: the **overtones**. They determine how an instrument sounds and explain why a violin sounds different from a clarinet.
wichtigste: The partials of a harmonic sound are whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency.
The first overtone lies an octave above the fundamental.
With a fundamental frequency of 110 Hz, the third partial has 330 Hz.
Instruments differ mainly in their overtone spectra.
A sine tone contains no overtones.
In overtone singing, such as the khöömei of Mongolia and Tuva, overtones are made audible.

abschnitte.text: A vibrating string does not vibrate only as a whole, but at the same time in halves, thirds, quarters and so on. Each of these vibrations produces a **partial**. The lowest is the **fundamental**, and the higher ones are called **overtones**. Their frequencies are **whole-number multiples** of the fundamental frequency: with 110 Hz, that means 220 Hz, 330 Hz, 440 Hz and so on.

The second partial, that is the **first overtone**, lies an **octave** above the fundamental. The third partial forms a fifth above that, and the fourth lies two octaves above the fundamental. Then come a major third and further, ever smaller steps. This series is called the **harmonic series** or overtone series.

If a **clarinet** and a **violin** play the same note, the fundamental is the same. What differs is which overtones sound along with it and how strongly: the **overtone spectrum**. This creates the **tone colour** (timbre). A pure **sine tone**, for example from a tone generator, has no overtones at all and therefore sounds very smooth and colourless.

The **alphorn** has no keys and no valves. On it you can play only the **natural notes**, that is the notes of the harmonic series. One of them sounds between F and F sharp and does not fit into any ordinary scale. It is called the **alphorn fa**. It gives many alphorn melodies their special sound.

In **overtone singing**, singers shape their mouth and throat so that individual overtones stand out like a second, whistling voice. It is traditionally widespread in **Mongolia** and in **Tuva**, where it is called **khöömei**. On string instruments, **harmonics** are produced when you touch the string only lightly at a node. Then a bright, glassy overtone sounds.

gewusst: On natural trumpets and hunting horns, too, only the notes of the harmonic series can be played.
With a little practice you can also pick out the quiet overtones that sound along when you sing normally.

teile.einleitung: **Eurhythmics** is a method of learning music with your whole body. You listen to music, move to it and in this way feel the beat, the tempo and the expression. It was founded by the Swiss music teacher Émile Jaques-Dalcroze.
wichtigste: Émile Jaques-Dalcroze founded eurhythmics, learning music through movement.
In 1915 he founded his institute for eurhythmics in Geneva.
When conducting, the hand goes down on the first beat of a bar.
The hand moves up for the last beat of a bar.
In the method of Zoltán Kodály a crotchet (quarter note) is spoken as “ta”.

abschnitte.text: **Émile Jaques-Dalcroze** was born in Vienna in 1865 and was Swiss. He taught at the conservatory in **Geneva** and noticed that many students could read rhythms but could not really feel them. So he had them walk, run and act out the music. This is how **eurhythmics** came about. In 1915 he founded his own **institute** in Geneva.

In eurhythmics you translate music into movement. If the music gets faster, you walk faster; if it gets quieter, you move more gently. In this way you learn **beat**, **tempo**, **dynamics** and form. Today the method is used all over the world in music schools, nursery schools and in therapy. In Switzerland you can study eurhythmics at universities of music.

Conductors also show rhythm with movement. On the **first beat** of a bar the hand always goes **down**. In 3/4 time a right-handed conductor moves the second beat **to the right** and the third upwards. The **last beat** of a bar always goes **up**, so that the hand is ready for the beginning of the next bar.

The Hungarian composer **Zoltán Kodály** developed a method in which children speak rhythms with syllables. A **crotchet** (quarter note) is called **“ta”**, two quavers (eighth notes) are called “ti-ti”. This way you can speak rhythms before you can read music. Similar syllable systems are used in many schools today.

gewusst: Before he returned to Geneva, Jaques-Dalcroze ran a school in Hellerau near Dresden for some years.
Jaques-Dalcroze also composed many songs and festival plays for French-speaking Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Rubin’s vase is a well-known ambiguous picture: you see either a vase or two faces looking at each other. It shows how our brain decides what is figure and what is background. The Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin described it around 1915.
wichtigste: You can see Rubin’s vase as a vase or as two faces.
It shows the figure-ground relationship.
The Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin described it around 1915.
You never see both images at the same time, only one after the other.
Pictures like this are called ambiguous or reversible figures.

abschnitte.text: In the middle of the picture there is a light shape that looks like a **vase**. To the left and right of it there is a dark area. If you look at the dark edges, you suddenly recognise two **faces** in profile looking at each other. The outlines of the vase are at the same time the outlines of the faces. The picture “flips” back and forth between the two interpretations.

Our brain divides every picture into **figure** and **ground**. The figure is what we pay attention to; it seems to be at the front. The ground is the background behind it. In Rubin’s vase, both areas fit equally well as the figure. That is why our perception switches, and we can only ever see one of the images at a time.

The figure-ground relationship is an important principle of **Gestalt psychology**, which studies how we perceive shapes. Artists such as the Dutchman M. C. Escher played with this effect. Graphic designers also sometimes hide a second image in the space between shapes in logos. Other well-known ambiguous pictures are the duck-rabbit and the Necker cube.

gewusst: A famous logo of a parcel delivery company hides an arrow in the space between two letters, exactly following the principle of figure and ground.

teile.einleitung: Swiss design is known for clear shapes, good quality and practical ideas. Many objects from Switzerland are world-famous, from the railway clock to the Swatch.
wichtigste: Swiss design is seen as simple, functional and precise.
The SBB railway clock by Hans Hilfiker is a design icon.
Fritz Haller developed the USM Haller furniture system.
Le Corbusier was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1887.
The Swatch came on the market in 1983.
The typeface Helvetica also comes from Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In 1944 Hans Hilfiker designed the SBB **railway clock**. Its red second hand has a special feature: it goes round a little faster than one minute and **stops briefly at the twelve**. There it waits for the minute pulse. Only then does the minute hand jump on, and the second hand starts again.

In the 1960s the architect **Fritz Haller** developed a furniture system for the company **USM** in Münsingen in the canton of Bern. It consists of steel tubes, connecting balls and metal panels. You can put the parts together in new ways again and again. Another classic is the aluminium **Landi chair** by Hans Coray for the 1939 National Exhibition.

**Le Corbusier** was born in 1887 as Charles-Édouard Jeanneret in **La Chaux-de-Fonds** in the Neuchâtel Jura. He became one of the most important architects of **modernism**. As well as houses, he also designed furniture, for example loungers and armchairs made of steel tubing. His picture appeared on Switzerland’s former ten-franc note.

In the 1970s the Swiss watch industry fell into the **quartz crisis**, because cheap quartz watches came from Asia. In 1983 the **Swatch** came on the market, an inexpensive plastic watch with only 51 parts. It was a great success. The typeface **Helvetica**, created in 1957 in Münchenstein near Basel, is also world-famous.

gewusst: The name Swatch is often explained as short for “Second Watch”.
The typeface Helvetica is still used today for many company logos and road signs all over the world.

teile.einleitung: Suva is the Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund, based in Lucerne. It insures many employees against accidents and works to make sure accidents do not happen in the first place.
wichtigste: Suva stands for Schweizerische Unfallversicherungsanstalt, the Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund.
It is based in Lucerne.
It insures employees against accidents and occupational diseases.
In Switzerland accident insurance is compulsory for employees.
Suva gives information about working safely, in workshops too.
It is an independent institution and does not aim to make a profit.

abschnitte.text: **Suva** is the **Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund**. It is based in **Lucerne** and began its work in 1918. In Switzerland all employees must be insured against **accidents**. Many businesses, especially in industry, building and crafts, are insured with Suva. Suva is an independent institution and is **not profit-oriented**.

If someone has an accident, the accident insurance pays, for example, for the doctor, hospital and therapy. If the person cannot work for a while, they receive part of their wages as a **daily allowance**. Accidents at work, **occupational accidents**, are insured. Anyone who works enough hours a week is also insured in their free time. **Occupational diseases**, which are caused by work, are also covered.

An important task of Suva is **prevention**, that is, preventing accidents. It publishes rules and information sheets on how to work safely. This includes, for example, wearing **safety glasses**, ear protection or a helmet. There are also clear rules for workshops and for handling machines. With campaigns, Suva also reminds people of dangers in their free time, for example in sport.

After a serious accident, Suva helps people to get well again. It runs its own **rehabilitation clinics**. There injured people practise moving again and coping with everyday life. The aim is for them to be able to work again.

gewusst: Employers, employees and the federal government are all represented on Suva’s highest board.
Apprentices in workshops often get to know Suva’s safety rules in their very first week.

teile.einleitung: St Gallen embroidery made eastern Switzerland world-famous around 1900. Fine lace and embroidered fabrics from St Gallen were sold all over the world. Today they are a luxury product of haute couture.
wichtigste: Josua Heilmann invented the hand embroidery machine in 1828.
Isaak Gröbli from Oberuzwil invented the shuttle embroidery machine in 1863.
Around 1910 embroidery was Switzerland’s largest export industry.
The First World War caused a great embroidery crisis in 1914.
The Textile Museum St Gallen shows lace, embroidery and pattern books.
Today international fashion houses buy St Gallen lace.

abschnitte.text: Eastern Switzerland had a long tradition with **linen** and later cotton. At first embroidery was done by hand, often as **work at home**. In 1828 **Josua Heilmann** from Mulhouse invented the **hand embroidery machine**. In eastern Switzerland it became the basis of industrial embroidery. In 1863 **Isaak Gröbli** from Oberuzwil invented the **shuttle embroidery machine**. It works with a shuttle like a sewing machine and is much faster.

At the end of the 19th century embroidery experienced an enormous **boom**. In many villages there were embroidery machines, in factories and in houses. Around 1910 embroidery made up about **18 per cent** of Swiss exports. This made it the country’s largest export industry. St Gallen produced more than half of all the embroidery in the world.

With the outbreak of the **First World War** in 1914, demand for luxury embroidery collapsed. Fashion also changed. The **Great Depression** made things even worse. Between 1920 and 1937 the number of embroidery machines fell from more than 13,000 to fewer than 2,000. Many people lost their jobs, and many machines were scrapped.

The industry survived by specialising in **high-quality niches**. Today international **haute couture** houses such as Dior or Chanel use St Gallen lace and embroidery. In the **Textile Museum St Gallen**, founded by the merchants’ guild, the Kaufmännische Corporation, you can see old lace and pattern books. In this way the history of St Gallen embroidery lives on.

gewusst: Magnificent buildings in St Gallen, the so-called embroidery palaces, were built with the money from embroidery.

teile.einleitung: Kerning, in German “Unterschneidung”, is a term from typography. It means adjusting the space between two particular letters. This makes a word look even and attractive.
wichtigste: In German, kerning is called Unterschneidung.
It changes the space between one particular pair of letters.
Typical pairs are “AV”, “To”, “LT” or “Wa”.
Tracking, on the other hand, changes the spacing evenly across the whole text.
Modern typefaces have built-in tables for kerning.

abschnitte.text: Every letter has its own shape. An “A” is narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, a “V” is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom. When they stand next to each other, a large gap appears, even though the measured distance is the same. Our eye then sees a hole in the word. **Kerning** moves such letters a little closer together so that the spacing looks **visually** balanced.

With **kerning** you only change the space of a single pair of letters. With **tracking**, in German “Laufweite”, you change the space between all the letters of a text evenly. Wider tracking is also called **letter-spacing**. Good designers pay attention to kerning especially in large headings and logos, because gaps are particularly noticeable there.

In the past, texts were set from individual metal letters, in **hot metal type**. So that two letters could move closer together, parts of a letter were cut so that they stuck out over the next one. That is where the German name “Unterschneidung”, undercutting, comes from. Today digital typefaces store, for many pairs of letters, how far they should move together. Word processing programs apply this automatically.

gewusst: A well-designed typeface can contain information for thousands of pairs of letters.

teile.einleitung: Clay is a fine, soft earth from nature. With water you can knead and shape it, and in the kiln it becomes as hard as stone. Pots, plates, figures and tiles have been made from clay for thousands of years.
wichtigste: Clay is made of tiny particles that come from weathered rock.
Damp clay is soft and easy to shape.
In the air, clay dries and becomes firm, but not yet waterproof.
Only in the kiln, at very high heat, does clay become as hard as stone.
Vessels are shaped by hand, with coils or on the potter’s wheel.
Glaze makes clay tableware smooth, shiny and watertight.
Fired clay is called ceramics.

abschnitte.text: Clay forms when rock is broken down over a very long time by water, wind and weather. What is left are tiny particles, much finer than sand. When water is added, these particles slide past each other. That is why damp clay is so **easy to shape**. So that it does not dry out, you cover it with a damp cloth or plastic.

There are different ways of making something out of clay. For a small bowl you press a hollow into a ball of clay with your thumb. In the **coil technique**, you roll long sausages of clay and lay them on top of each other in a circle. You smooth the coils together well so that nothing falls apart. In the slab technique you cut flat slabs of clay and put them together like a box.

On the **potter’s wheel** a lump of clay spins quickly round and round. With wet hands you press it into the centre and then pull the walls up. This is how round bowls, cups and vases are made. It takes a lot of practice. Someone who makes vessels from clay is a **potter**, today often also called a ceramicist.

Dried clay breaks easily and softens again in water. That is why it is fired in the **kiln**, at temperatures often above 900 degrees. That is much hotter than an oven in the kitchen. Then the **glaze** is applied and the piece is fired a second time. The glaze melts into a smooth, glassy and often coloured layer.

gewusst: The word “terracotta” comes from Italian and means “baked earth”.
Roof tiles and bricks for houses are also fired from clay.
In Switzerland, for example, the painted pottery from Heimberg and Langnau in the canton of Bern is well known.

teile.einleitung: In subtractive colour mixing you mix colouring substances, for example in the paint box or in a printer. Each colour absorbs part of the light. The more colours you mix, the darker it gets.
wichtigste: Subtractive means that something is taken away.
Colouring substances absorb part of the light and reflect the rest.
The primary colours are cyan, magenta and yellow.
If you mix all three, you get a dark brown or black.
In printing, CMYK stands for cyan, magenta, yellow and key.
The key plate prints black.

abschnitte.text: White light contains all colours. When it hits a layer of paint, the paint **absorbs** part of it. Only the rest is reflected and reaches our eye. A yellow paint, for example, absorbs blue light. Because light is taken away in the process, this kind of mixing is called **subtractive**, from the Latin word for taking away.

The primary colours of subtractive mixing are **cyan**, a light blue-green, **magenta**, a strong pink, and **yellow**. If you mix cyan and yellow, you get green. Magenta and yellow make red. If you mix all three, almost all the light is absorbed and you get a very dark shade. By contrast, in **additive colour mixing** with light, it keeps getting brighter.

Printers and print works use the **CMYK** colour model. It stands for cyan, magenta, yellow and **key**. The key plate prints **black** and provides the depth and the fine lines. The three coloured inks together do not make a rich black, but a muddy dark brown. Black also saves expensive coloured ink.

If you look at a printed picture through a **magnifying glass**, you see tiny dots in the four colours. These dots are called the **halftone screen**. From a distance they merge in the eye into all kinds of shades. In this way colour photos in newspapers and books are made from only four printing inks.

gewusst: The name key comes from the fact that the black plate used to serve as the key plate, to which the other colours were lined up.
A screen, on the other hand, mixes additively with red, green and blue light, RGB for short.

teile.einleitung: The right to your own image means that, in principle, every person may decide for themselves whether photos or videos of them are taken and published. In Switzerland it is part of the protection of personality in the Civil Code. This is especially important on social media.
wichtigste: The right to your own image is part of the protection of personality.
In Switzerland the basis is Article 28 of the Civil Code, ZGB for short.
Anyone who publishes a recognisable person without consent may violate their personality.
That is why you ask before posting whether the person in the picture agrees.
For public figures, some exceptions apply to their public appearances.

abschnitte.text: A photo shows what someone looks like, where they were and what they did. That is why your own image is part of your **personality**. The **Civil Code** protects personality in Article 28 against unlawful violations. So anyone who publishes a picture of a **recognisable** person usually needs their **consent**. Anyone whose rights have been violated can ask a court to have the picture removed.

Putting a photo of friends in a class chat or on a social network is publishing it. So before you post, you ask the people in the picture. You should never pass on embarrassing or hurtful pictures, not even “just for fun”. With children, the parents often have a say, but older children and teenagers can also decide for themselves. Many schools ask for consent before putting class photos on their website.

Not every picture needs permission. Someone who can be seen by chance as a small figure in a large crowd is not the focus. With well-known people such as politicians or sports stars, the media may report on public appearances with pictures. But their private lives remain protected. In each case, courts weigh up what matters more: the public interest or the protection of the person.

gewusst: In Switzerland, secret recordings of someone’s private life can even be a criminal offence.

teile.einleitung: A screw is a fastener with a spiral thread. When you turn it, the screw pulls itself into the material and holds firmly there. Unlike a nail, it can also be undone again.
wichtigste: The spiral groove on a screw is called the thread.
The thread pulls the screw into the material as you turn it.
Near the edge of hard wood you drill a pilot hole so that the wood does not split.
Most screws are tightened clockwise.
There are different drives such as slotted, cross-head, hexagon socket and hexalobular.
The hexalobular drive, often called Torx, has a six-pointed star.

abschnitte.text: A screw consists of the **head** and the **shank**. The **thread**, a spiral groove, winds around the shank. When you turn it, the thread grips the material and pulls the screw in, rather like a sloping ramp wrapped around a rod. That is why a screw holds more firmly than a nail. And you can unscrew it again without damaging anything.

**Wood screws** have a point and cut their own thread into the wood. In doing so the screw pushes the wood fibres apart. Near the edge or in hard wood, the wood can therefore **split**. A small **pilot hole** prevents this. **Machine screws**, on the other hand, have a fine thread and are screwed into a nut or a threaded hole. In walls you usually need a **wall plug** so that the screw holds.

The **drive** is the shape in the screw head that the tool grips. The simplest is the **slot**, but the screwdriver slips out of it easily. With a **cross-head**, the tool grips better. The **hexagon socket** is turned with a six-sided key. With the **hexalobular** drive, often called Torx, the tool grips a star with six rounded points and slips out especially rarely.

Almost all screws have a **right-hand thread**. You tighten them clockwise and loosen them anticlockwise. A little rhyme helps: righty tighty, lefty loosey. But there are also left-hand threads, for example on the left pedal of a bike, so that it does not come loose by itself while riding. It is always important that the screwdriver fits the drive exactly.

gewusst: The Archimedes screw uses a large thread to lift water uphill and is more than 2,000 years old.
The Torx screw was developed in the USA in the 1960s.

teile.einleitung: Serifs are the small finishing strokes on the letters of some typefaces. They are an important feature for telling typefaces apart.
wichtigste: Serifs are small crossbars at the ends of the strokes of letters.
They are also called little feet.
Times is a well-known typeface with serifs.
Typefaces without serifs are called sans serif or grotesque.
Helvetica from Switzerland is a sans serif typeface.

abschnitte.text: If you look closely at a capital T in a newspaper typeface, you can see fine **crossbars** at the ends. These are called **serifs**. They sit at the top and bottom of the strokes of the letters. Many people also call them little feet. Well-known typefaces with serifs are **Times** and **Garamond**.

Serifs can already be found in old **Roman inscriptions** in stone. When the letters were carved, small widenings formed at the ends. Later, scribes and printers took over this shape. Typefaces in this tradition are called **roman** typefaces, in German “Antiqua”. They are still often used for books and newspapers today.

Typefaces without serifs are called **sans serif** or **grotesque**. They look simple and modern. One of the best known is **Helvetica**, which was created in Switzerland in 1957. Sans serif typefaces are often used on screens, signs and posters. Which kind is easier to read depends on size, purpose and design.

gewusst: The word grotesque comes from the fact that typefaces without serifs used to seem strange to many people.
The lettering on Swiss motorway signs is also sans serif, so that it can be read quickly.

teile.einleitung: Modern art is the name for the art from about 1900 that broke with old rules and went completely new ways. Instead of showing the world true to nature, artists experimented with wild colours, angular shapes, chance and everyday objects. Some works caused great excitement at the time and are world-famous today.
wichtigste: Modern art includes many new art movements that arose from about 1900.
In 1905 Kirchner, Heckel and Schmidt-Rottluff founded the artists’ group “Die Brücke” (The Bridge) in Dresden.
From 1907/08 Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque developed Cubism.
In 1912 Kandinsky and Marc published the almanac “Der Blaue Reiter” (The Blue Rider) in Munich.
Dadaism was founded in 1916 at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich.
Marcel Duchamp declared everyday objects to be works of art and called them readymades.
Paul Klee was born in 1879 in Münchenbuchsee near Bern and taught at the Bauhaus.

abschnitte.text: **Modern art** is an umbrella term for the many new art movements that arose from about 1900. Photography could now show reality, so painting looked for new tasks. Artists wanted to show feelings, ideas, movement or pure colours and shapes. Art from about 1960 to today is usually called **contemporary art**.

In 1905 Henri Matisse and his friends exhibited pictures with garish, unnatural colours at the Paris Autumn Salon. A critic called them **“Fauves”**, meaning wild beasts. In the same year Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Erich Heckel and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff founded the group **Die Brücke** in Dresden. In 1912 Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc published the almanac “Der Blaue Reiter” in Munich.

In 1907 **Pablo Picasso** painted “Les Demoiselles d’Avignon”, a key work on the way to Cubism. Together with Georges Braque he broke objects down into angular shapes and showed them from several angles. In Italy, Filippo Tommaso Marinetti published the manifesto of **Futurism** in 1909. The Futurists celebrated speed, technology, cars and machines.

In 1916, in the middle of the First World War, Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings opened the **Cabaret Voltaire** in the Spiegelgasse in Zurich. This is where **Dadaism** began, a movement that protested against war and rigid rules with nonsense poems, noise and chance. The Dadaists also included Tristan Tzara, Hans Arp, Marcel Janco and Sophie Taeuber-Arp. The Cabaret Voltaire still exists today.

**Marcel Duchamp** declared factory-made everyday objects to be art and called them **readymades**. In 1917 he submitted a urinal titled “Fountain” to an exhibition, which caused a scandal. At the same time **abstract art** appeared, which no longer shows any objects at all, for example with Kandinsky, Piet Mondrian or Kazimir Malevich. From 1924 the Surrealists painted dreamlike worlds.

**Paul Klee** was born in 1879 in Münchenbuchsee near Bern and created his own poetic visual language with lines, signs and fields of colour. From 1921 to 1931 he taught at the **Bauhaus**, a famous art school in Germany. Today the Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern shows around 4,000 of his works. In Switzerland you can also see modern art, for example, in the Kunsthaus Zürich, the Kunstmuseum Basel and the Fondation Beyeler.

begriffe.erklaerung: Artists who go new and unfamiliar ways, like the vanguard of an army.
An art movement from Zurich that protested against war and rules with nonsense and chance.
An everyday object that an artist declares to be a work of art.
A public statement in which a group of artists sets down its ideas.

gewusst: The name “Dada” is said to have been picked at random from a dictionary; in French it means hobby horse.
The original of Duchamp’s “Fountain” was lost; today there are only replicas from later years.
At the Cabaret Voltaire, Hugo Ball performed sound poems in a costume made of cardboard.

teile.einleitung: Silk is a shiny, fine natural fibre. It comes from the caterpillar of a moth, the silkworm moth. For thousands of years silk has been a precious fabric.
wichtigste: Silk is spun by the caterpillar of the domestic silk moth.
The caterpillar eats the leaves of the mulberry tree.
Its cocoon consists of a single thread several hundred metres long.
Silk is the only natural fibre that occurs as a continuous thread.
Silk making comes from China.
The Silk Road was an important trade route between Asia and Europe.

abschnitte.text: Silk comes from the caterpillar of the **domestic silk moth**, a night-flying moth. The caterpillar eats almost only **mulberry leaves** and grows quickly. When it is big enough, it spins itself into a **cocoon**. To do this, it squeezes a fine thread out of glands on its head. Inside the cocoon it turns into a pupa.

A cocoon consists of a single thread **several hundred metres** long. A thread like this is called a **filament** or continuous thread. The cocoons are soaked in hot water so that the thread comes loose. Then several threads are unwound together. Other natural fibres such as wool or cotton, on the other hand, are short fibres that have to be spun into yarn.

Silk making was invented in **China** and kept secret for a long time. Merchants brought the fabrics along the **Silk Road** as far as Europe. In the 6th century silkworms reached the Byzantine Empire. Later, silk was also made in Italy and France. In Switzerland, **Zurich** was an important silk city in the 19th century.

Silk is **light**, shines beautifully and feels smooth. It keeps you warm in winter and cool in summer. Silk is made of **protein**, similar to hair. That is why you wash it gently and not too hot. Silk is used for dresses, ties, scarves and, in the past, also for parachutes.

gewusst: A single silk scarf needs a great many cocoons.
Today the silkworm moth can only survive with human help, because it has been bred for so long.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss pocket knife, called “Sackmesser” in Switzerland, is known all over the world. With its red handle and the Swiss cross, it stands for quality and inventiveness.
wichtigste: Karl Elsener opened a cutlery workshop in Ibach SZ in 1884.
From 1891 he supplied soldier’s knives to the Swiss Army.
In 1897 he registered the officer’s and sports knife.
The name Victorinox combines Victoria and “inox”.
Wenger from Delémont has belonged to Victorinox since 2005.
In Switzerland people usually say “Sackmesser”.

abschnitte.text: **Karl Elsener** opened a cutlery workshop in **Ibach** in the canton of Schwyz in 1884. At that time the Swiss Army still bought its soldier’s knives abroad. Elsener wanted to change that. At the end of 1891 he began making **soldier’s knives** for the army. In doing so he laid the foundation for a world-famous product.

In 1897 Elsener registered the **officer’s and sports knife**. What was special about it: the tools lay on **both sides of the handle** and were held by just one spring. This meant more functions fitted into a small knife. Later, tools such as scissors, a saw, a screwdriver and a corkscrew were added. The pocket knife became a versatile tool for your trouser pocket.

Karl Elsener named his company after his mother **Victoria**. Later the word **“inox”** was added, which stands for stainless steel. This is how the name **Victorinox** came about. To this day the company is based in Ibach and is one of the best-known Swiss brands.

The company **Wenger** in **Delémont** in the Jura also made army knives. For a long time the two companies shared the army’s orders. In 2005 Victorinox took over Wenger. The Wenger brand was then integrated into the Victorinox group. Since then the two traditional pocket knife makers have belonged together.

gewusst: In English the pocket knife is called the “Swiss Army Knife”, the knife of the Swiss army.
Swiss pocket knives have even travelled into space with astronauts.

teile.einleitung: Paul Klee was one of the best-known painters of the 20th century. He was born near Bern in 1879 and painted colourful, playful and often mysterious pictures. In Bern the Zentrum Paul Klee is a reminder of him.
wichtigste: Paul Klee was born in 1879 in Münchenbuchsee near Bern and died in Ticino in 1940.
He came from a family of musicians and played the violin excellently.
On his trip to Tunis in 1914 he discovered colour for himself.
He taught for many years at the Bauhaus in Germany.
He created almost 10,000 works.
The Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern was built by Renzo Piano and opened in 2005.

abschnitte.text: Paul Klee was born on 18 December 1879 in **Münchenbuchsee** near Bern. His father was a music teacher, his mother a singer. Paul played the **violin** very well and made music all his life. For a long time he did not know whether to become a musician or a painter. He chose art and studied in Munich. But music remained important: many of his pictures seem like rhythms and sounds made of colour.

In 1914 Klee travelled with the painters **August Macke** and **Louis Moilliet** to **Tunis** in North Africa. The bright light and glowing colours made a strong impression on him. In his diary he wrote that he and colour were now one; he was a painter. From this trip on, colour played a much greater part in his pictures. He made many small watercolours with coloured areas.

From 1921 to 1931 Klee taught at the **Bauhaus**, a famous school of art and design in Germany. After that he taught at the art academy in Düsseldorf. When the **Nazis** came to power in 1933, he lost his job and his art was persecuted as unwanted. So Klee moved back to Bern with his family. There he went on painting to the very end, despite a serious illness.

Klee rarely just copied what he saw. He invented signs, lines, arrows and patterns and built figures, cities and landscapes out of them. His pictures are often small, but full of ideas and humour. Well-known examples are “Senecio”, a face made of coloured fields, and “Ad Parnassum”. In all he created almost **10,000 works**. He died on 29 June 1940 in Muralto in Ticino.

The **Zentrum Paul Klee** has stood in Bern since 2005. The Italian architect **Renzo Piano** designed it with three wave-shaped roofs that remind you of a landscape of hills. The museum has the largest collection of Klee’s works in the world. As well as exhibitions, there is a children’s museum where children can create things themselves.

gewusst: Although Klee was connected with Switzerland almost all his life, he had German citizenship because of his father.
Klee once wrote, roughly, that art does not reproduce the visible, but makes visible.

teile.einleitung: **Note values** show how long a note sounds. You can recognise them by what the note looks like: by its head, its stem and its flags. For every note there is also a rest that lasts the same length of time.
wichtigste: A semibreve (whole note) has a white head and no stem.
A minim (half note) has a white head with a stem and lasts two beats in 4/4 time.
A crotchet (quarter note) has a black head with a stem and lasts one beat.
A quaver (eighth note) has one flag, a semiquaver (sixteenth note) two.
A minim lasts as long as two crotchets.
A crotchet can be divided into four semiquavers.

abschnitte.text: The **semibreve** (whole note) is a white head without a stem. In 4/4 time it lasts four beats, so a whole bar. The **minim** (half note) has a white head and a **stem**. It lasts half as long, so in 4/4 time **two beats**. Two minims fill a bar of 4/4.

The **crotchet** (quarter note) has a black head with a stem and lasts one beat. Two crotchets are as long as one minim. The **quaver** (eighth note) also has a **flag** on its stem; two quavers make one crotchet. The **semiquaver** (sixteenth note) has two flags. Four semiquavers together make one crotchet.

If several quavers or semiquavers stand next to each other, their stems are often joined with **beams**. One beam replaces one flag, two beams replace two flags. This makes it easier to see the beats in the bar. It does not change the sound.

For every note value there is a **rest** of the same length. The **semibreve rest** is a small block hanging below a line. The **minim rest** looks similar but sits on the line and lasts as long as a minim. The **crotchet rest** is a zigzag sign and lasts **one beat**. Quaver and semiquaver rests have little hooks like flags.

A **dot** after a note lengthens it by half its value. So a dotted minim lasts three beats, namely two plus one. A dotted crotchet lasts one and a half beats. Such dotted notes appear in many songs and give them swing.

gewusst: Memory aid: the semibreve rest hangs down like a heavy hat, the minim rest sits like a hat on a head.
There are even demisemiquavers (thirty-second notes) and even shorter notes with three or more flags.

teile.einleitung: The saw is one of the most important tools in the workshop. With its sharp teeth it cuts through wood, plastic or metal. There is a suitable saw for every job.
wichtigste: A saw cuts with lots of small, sharp teeth.
Sawing produces fine sawdust.
The wood must be held firmly with a clamp or in a vice.
With a fretsaw you cut fine curves.
The panel saw is a hand saw for straight cuts.
Safety glasses protect your eyes.

abschnitte.text: The **saw blade** has lots of small, sharp **teeth**. As you move it back and forth, each tooth tears out a tiny piece of wood. In this way the saw works its way through the material bit by bit. The torn-out bits of wood fall down as fine **sawdust**. The teeth are bent slightly to the side so that the blade does not jam in the cut.

The **panel saw** is a hand saw with a wide blade for straight cuts through boards. In German it is called “Fuchsschwanz”, fox’s tail, because its shape is reminiscent of a fox’s tail. The **fretsaw** has a very thin blade in a frame. With it you saw curves and figures out of thin **plywood**. For metal there is the **hacksaw** with very fine teeth.

Before sawing, you draw a line with a **pencil** and ruler. That way the cut is straight and in the right place. Then you hold the wood firmly with a **clamp** or in the **vice**. Otherwise it slips away and you can hurt yourself. You saw just next to the line so that the workpiece does not end up too small.

When sawing, small bits of wood can fly about. **Safety glasses** protect your eyes from them. You always keep your free hand away from the saw blade. Children may only use electric saws such as a circular saw or jigsaw under supervision. After working, you sweep up the sawdust so that nobody slips.

gewusst: Japanese saws cut when you pull and not when you push. That is why their blades can be very thin.
Sawdust is used, for example, as bedding for animals or for wood pellets.

teile.einleitung: The **circle of fifths** arranges all the major and minor keys in a circle. Neighbouring keys are a fifth apart and differ by only one sharp or flat. So you can see at a glance how many sharps or flats a key has.
wichtigste: Neighbouring major keys are a perfect fifth apart.
Going clockwise, one sharp is added each time: G major 1, D major 2, A major 3, E major 4, B major 5.
Going anticlockwise, flats are added: F major 1, B flat major 2, E flat major 3, A flat major 4.
The first three sharps are F sharp, C sharp and G sharp.
E minor has one sharp, G minor two flats.
F sharp major and G flat major sound the same on the piano.

abschnitte.text: At the top of the circle is **C major** with no sharps or flats. If you go clockwise up a **perfect fifth**, you get G major with one sharp, then **D major with two sharps**, A major with three, E major with four and **B major with five** sharps. Going anticlockwise you go down a fifth: F major with one flat, B flat major with two, E flat major with three and **A flat major with four flats**.

The sharps are always written in the same order: **F sharp, C sharp, G sharp**, D sharp, A sharp, E sharp. They, too, are each a fifth apart. A well-known German memory sentence for the sharp keys is “Geh Du Alter Esel Hole Fische” (“Go, you old donkey, fetch fish”), standing for G, D, A, E, H, F sharp; in German the note B is called H. The last sharp is always a semitone below the keynote of the major key.

The flats come in the reverse order: B flat, E flat, A flat, D flat, G flat, C flat. With the flat keys there is a handy trick: the second-to-last flat names the keynote. If a key has B flat, E flat and A flat, it is E flat major. Only F major, with a single flat, has to be memorised.

In the circle of fifths each major key has its **relative minor** with the same key signature. It lies a minor third lower. That is why **E minor**, like G major, has **one sharp**, and **G minor**, like B flat major, has **two flats**. Usually the minor keys are on the inside of the circle and the major keys on the outside.

At the bottom the two sides meet. **F sharp major** with six sharps and **G flat major** with six flats sound the same on the piano; they are only written differently. This is called **enharmonic equivalence**. Because of this the row of fifths closes into a circle with twelve major keys.

gewusst: Keys that lie close together in the circle of fifths share many notes. That is why pieces of music often change into a neighbouring key.
Twelve fifths stacked on top of each other make almost exactly seven octaves, but only almost.

teile.einleitung: Softwood comes from trees that have needles instead of leaves. These include spruce, fir, pine, larch and Swiss stone pine. In Switzerland softwood is a very important wood for building and crafts.
wichtigste: Conifers have needles and usually cones.
The **spruce** is a conifer; beech, oak and maple are broadleaved trees.
The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests.
Softwood is usually light, soft and rich in resin.
The larch is the only native conifer that loses its needles in autumn.
Softwood is used for houses, roof frames, furniture and paper.

abschnitte.text: Conifers have narrow, hard **needles** instead of broad leaves. Most of them stay green all year round. Their seeds grow in **cones**. Native conifers include spruce, silver fir, Scots pine, larch, Swiss stone pine and yew. Broadleaved trees such as **beech**, oak and maple, on the other hand, have leaves.

Spruce and fir look similar, but you can tell them apart. The needles of the **spruce** are pointed and prickly. The needles of the **silver fir** are softer and have two pale stripes underneath. Spruce cones hang downwards and fall to the ground whole. Fir cones stand upright on the branches and fall apart while still on the tree.

Softwood is usually **light** and fairly soft. That is why it is easy to saw, plane and nail. It often contains a lot of **resin**, which smells pleasant. Conifers grow faster than many broadleaved trees and have a straight trunk. So you get long, straight beams. One exception is the **yew**: its wood is very hard, and almost all parts of the tree are poisonous.

The **spruce** is the most common tree in Swiss forests. Its wood is used for roof frames, beams, planks and paper. **Larch** wood is very weatherproof and is suitable for house fronts and fences. **Swiss stone pine** wood is used, above all in the Grisons and Valais, to build parlours and furniture. It smells pleasant for a long time.

gewusst: The larch is a conifer that turns golden yellow in autumn and then sheds all its needles.
In the Alps, Swiss stone pines can grow right up to the tree line and live for several hundred years.

teile.einleitung: Street art is art in public spaces, that is, on streets, walls and squares. It includes graffiti, large wall paintings, pasted-up pictures and even knitting.
wichtigste: Street art is created in public spaces.
Harald Naegeli became known as the “Sprayer of Zurich”.
A tag is a sprayer’s quickly sprayed signature.
A mural is a large painting on the front of a building.
Keith Haring drew with chalk in the New York subway.
Painting on other people’s walls without permission is forbidden.

abschnitte.text: The best-known form of street art is **graffiti**, which is painted with spray cans. The simplest form is the **tag**, a sprayer’s personal signature. There are also large, colourful pictures with artistic letters. Graffiti without permission counts as **criminal damage** and is forbidden. That is why many cities offer legal walls where you are allowed to spray.

At the end of the 1970s, **Harald Naegeli** sprayed stick figures on walls in Zurich at night. He became known as the **“Sprayer of Zurich”**. Because he sprayed without permission, he was convicted. Later, however, he was also honoured as an artist. His case is still used today to discuss where art ends and damage to property begins.

A **mural** is a large painting on the front of a house. The word comes from the Latin **“murus”** for wall. Murals are usually painted legally, as commissions. **Paste-ups** are posters or paper pictures that are made at home and stuck onto walls with paste. In this way even large pictures can be put up quickly.

In **urban knitting**, also called yarn bombing, trees or railings are wrapped in knitting. It can easily be removed again. In **reverse graffiti** nothing is sprayed on; instead, dirt is deliberately cleaned off a wall. The picture is made by the clean areas. In the 1980s the New York artist **Keith Haring** drew figures with white chalk on empty black advertising spaces in the subway.

gewusst: The best-known street artist in the world calls himself Banksy, and nobody knows for sure who he is.
Keith Haring’s simple, lively figures later became world-famous on T-shirts and posters.

teile.einleitung: A loom is a device for weaving fabric. It keeps the warp threads tightly stretched and helps you pass the crosswise thread through quickly. From the simple wooden frame to the modern weaving machine, the loom has a long history.
wichtigste: The warp threads are wound on the warp beam.
The finished fabric is wound onto the cloth beam.
The shuttle carries the crosswise thread through the warp.
The reed presses each new weft thread against the fabric.
With pedals you raise and lower the warp threads.
The Jacquard loom was controlled by punched cards.

abschnitte.text: On the **warp beam**, a roller, is the supply of lengthwise threads. The warp threads run through small eyes, the **heddles**, which hang on frames called **shafts**. When you tread on the **pedals**, some shafts rise and the shed opens. At the other end the finished fabric is wound onto the **cloth beam**. In this way you can weave very long lengths of fabric.

The **shuttle** looks like a little boat and carries a bobbin with the thread. You push or throw it from one side to the other through the open shed. Then you press the new thread firmly into place with the **reed**. The reed is a comb-like part through which the warp threads run. This step is called **beating**.

For a long time weaving was done only by hand, often at home as **cottage work**. In the 18th century John Kay invented the **flying shuttle**, which could be sent shooting through the shed with a jerk. Soon after came mechanical looms driven by water power or steam engines. They were among the most important machines of **industrialisation**. In Switzerland, too, for example in the Zurich Oberland and the Glarus area, many weaving mills were built.

Around 1805 the Frenchman Joseph-Marie Jacquard presented a special loom. It was controlled by **punched cards**. The holes decided which warp threads were raised. This made it possible to weave complicated patterns automatically. The idea of controlling a machine with punched cards was later also used for early **calculating machines** and computers.

gewusst: In the 20th century the company Sulzer in Winterthur built weaving machines that were sold all over the world.
In Switzerland there are museums where old looms are still demonstrated.

teile.einleitung: In a parallel circuit, several devices are connected so that each has its own path for the current. If one fails, the others keep working. The lamps and sockets in a flat, for example, are connected like this.
wichtigste: In a parallel circuit each device has its own path for the current.
If one lamp fails, the others keep shining.
All devices connected in parallel get the same voltage.
The total current is the sum of the individual currents.
Lamps and sockets in homes are connected in parallel.

abschnitte.text: In a **parallel circuit**, the circuit branches. Each lamp lies in its own **branch** between the same two wires. The current divides and flows through all the branches at the same time. If one lamp breaks, only its branch is interrupted. The other lamps stay lit.

Each device has the same **voltage** across it; in a Swiss socket that is 230 volts. Each device takes as much **current** as it needs. The currents of all the branches add up to the total current. If too many powerful devices are plugged into one multi-socket adaptor, the total current becomes too large. Then the **fuse** switches off so that the wire does not get too hot.

In a home, all the lamps and sockets are connected in parallel. That is why you can switch off the television without the lights going out. The opposite is the **series circuit**, in which all the devices lie one after another on a single path. There everything goes out if one part fails.

gewusst: The more devices you connect in parallel, the smaller the total resistance of the circuit becomes.

teile.einleitung: The history of music tells how music developed from the first bone flutes to pop and streaming. It is divided into eras, for example the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, the Baroque, the Classical period and Romanticism. Each era has its own sound, its own instruments and famous composers.
wichtigste: The oldest known musical instruments are flutes made of bone that are over 35000 years old.
In the Middle Ages people sang the single-line Latin Gregorian chant in churches.
In the 11th century Guido of Arezzo developed the syllables ut, re, mi for learning to sing.
The Baroque era began around 1600, and it was followed by the Classical period.
Frédéric Chopin and Robert Schumann belong to Romanticism.
In 1877 Thomas Edison invented the phonograph for recording sound.
The melody of the Swiss Psalm was created by Alberik Zwyssig.

abschnitte.text: Even people in the Stone Age made music. In caves in the Swabian Jura in Germany, **bone flutes** made of bird bones and mammoth ivory were found that are over 35000 years old. Music also played a big role in the ancient civilisations such as Egypt, China and Greece. The ancient Greeks were already thinking about scales and the number ratios between notes.

In the Middle Ages, from about 500 to 1400, music was closely linked to the Church. Monks sang **Gregorian chant**, a single-line song in Latin. In the 11th century the Benedictine monk Guido of Arezzo developed the syllables ut, re, mi, which later became do, re, mi, and improved the lines used for writing music. Hildegard of Bingen, a nun from the 12th century, is one of the first composers known by name. Around 1200 Léonin and Pérotin of the **Notre-Dame school** in Paris created early music in several parts, and in the 14th century Guillaume de Machaut composed the “Messe de Nostre Dame”.

In the Renaissance, from about 1400 to 1600, music gained more parts and a fuller sound, and from 1501 music could be printed. Around 1600 the **Baroque** began, the era in which opera was invented. Well-known composers of this time are Claudio Monteverdi, Antonio Vivaldi with “The Four Seasons”, George Frideric Handel and Johann Sebastian Bach. Typical is the **basso continuo**, a continuous accompanying part in the low register.

After Bach's death in 1750 came the **Classical period** with Joseph Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and Ludwig van Beethoven, who mostly worked in Vienna. Music became clearer, and the symphony and the string quartet became important. In the 19th century came **Romanticism**, to which Frédéric Chopin, Robert Schumann, Franz Schubert and Richard Wagner belong. During this time, in 1841 to be exact, the Cistercian monk Alberik Zwyssig composed the melody of what later became the Swiss Psalm at Wettingen Abbey.

In 1877 Thomas Edison invented the **phonograph**, with which sounds could be recorded and played back for the first time. After that came the record, radio, tape, CD and finally streaming. At the same time completely new styles appeared, such as jazz, rock, pop, hip-hop and electronic music. In classical music composers such as Stravinsky and Schoenberg searched for new sounds; this is called **New Music**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A longer period of time with typical features.
Single-line Latin church singing of the Middle Ages.
Singing with syllables such as do, re, mi instead of note names.
A low accompanying part in the Baroque, above which chords are played.
The first device for recording and playing back sounds.

gewusst: The Abbey Library of St Gallen owns some of the oldest surviving music manuscripts with early musical signs.
The syllable ut was later replaced by do because it is easier to sing.
On Edison's first recording he himself sang the nursery rhyme “Mary Had a Little Lamb”.

teile.einleitung: Fashion is the way people dress at a particular time. It is always changing and shows what is popular at the moment. Some fashion inventions, such as jeans or the little black dress, are still with us today.
wichtigste: **Haute couture** is made-to-measure clothing made by hand, above all in Paris.
**Prêt-à-porter** means “ready to wear” and is made in standard sizes.
In 1873 Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented work trousers strengthened with rivets.
The name denim goes back to the French town of Nîmes.
Coco Chanel made the “little black dress” popular in the 1920s.
Eastern Switzerland is known for its embroidery and textiles.

abschnitte.text: **Haute couture** is the highest art of dressmaking. In Paris fashion houses, clothes are made by hand and exactly to measure for individual customers. This takes a long time and is very expensive. **Prêt-à-porter**, on the other hand, means “ready to wear”. These clothes are made in standard sizes and sold in shops. This is also called **off-the-peg** clothing.

In 1873 **Levi Strauss** and the tailor **Jacob Davis** patented special work trousers in the USA. Small metal **rivets** strengthened the pockets so that they did not tear. The trousers were meant for gold diggers and workers. From them came **blue jeans**. In the 20th century they became the favourite trousers of young people all over the world.

Jeans fabric is called **denim**. The name comes from “serge de Nîmes”, a fabric from the French town of **Nîmes**. Denim is a so-called **twill fabric**. The lengthwise threads are dyed blue and the crosswise threads are white. That is why denim is blue on the outside and lighter on the inside.

In 1926 the French fashion designer **Coco Chanel** presented a simple, short black dress. Until then black had been seen mainly as the colour of mourning. Chanel’s dress was simple, comfortable and elegant. The **“little black dress”** became a classic that still exists today in many forms. Chanel also shaped a fashion that gave women more freedom of movement in other ways.

The **St Gallen** region has long been known for its **embroidery** and fine fabrics. These fabrics are also used by big fashion houses in Paris. Today a lot of clothing is made cheaply and in large quantities. This is called **fast fashion**. It is much discussed, because it creates a lot of waste and working conditions are often poor.

gewusst: The first jeans did not yet have belt loops, but buttons for braces.
The word “mode”, as in the French and German words for fashion, comes from the Latin “modus”, which means manner or way.

teile.einleitung: An object poster shows only what matters: a single product and the brand name. This clear form of advertising began in Berlin at the start of the 20th century. In Switzerland it was developed further by well-known graphic designers.
wichtigste: An object poster shows a single product and the brand name.
It does without stories, figures and lots of text.
Lucian Bernhard, who designed posters like this in Berlin from 1905, is seen as its founder.
Large areas of colour and clear lettering make it easy to read from a distance.
In Switzerland, Niklaus Stoecklin and Herbert Leupin took up this form.

abschnitte.text: Many posters around 1900 were full of flourishes, figures and text. The **object poster** did things differently: it shows only the **product** and, above or below it, the **brand name**. The background is usually a simple area of colour. That way you get the message even when walking past or from a moving tram. Advertising became clearer and more modern as a result.

The graphic designer **Lucian Bernhard** is seen as the founder of the object poster. From 1905 he designed posters in Berlin that made do with a few colours and large shapes. His poster for a brand of matches, which shows only two matches and the name, is well known. This style was quickly copied in Germany.

In Switzerland graphic designers developed the object poster further, especially in **Basel**. **Niklaus Stoecklin** painted products so precisely and glossily that they looked almost real. **Herbert Leupin** also designed object posters and later witty, playful advertising posters too. Swiss posters became known internationally. Today many of them are kept in the poster collection of the Museum für Gestaltung in Zurich.

gewusst: In Switzerland posters are often hung in the “world format”, which measures 89.5 by 128 centimetres.

teile.einleitung: Site-specific art is art that is created for a particular place. It includes the architecture, the history or the landscape of that place. If you move it somewhere else, it loses its meaning.
wichtigste: Site-specific art is called “ortsspezifische Kunst” in German.
It is created for a particular place and only works properly there.
It arose mainly from the 1960s and 1970s.
**Land art** creates works directly in the landscape.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped buildings and landscapes for a short time.
When the Swiss federal government builds new buildings, art is often planned in.

abschnitte.text: Most pictures can be taken from one museum to another. With **site-specific art** it is different. The artists create the work for one particular place. They include the **architecture**, the history or the landscape of that place. In another place the work would lose its meaning.

In the 1960s and 1970s some artists went out of the museums into nature. They created works from earth, stones or water directly in the landscape. This is called **land art**. A famous example is the **“Spiral Jetty”** by Robert Smithson from 1970. It is a huge spiral of stones in the Great Salt Lake in the USA.

The artist couple **Christo and Jeanne-Claude** wrapped buildings, bridges and landscapes in fabric. The wrapped **Reichstag** in Berlin in 1995 is famous. Their works only stood for a short time. They changed the way people saw well-known places. In Switzerland, at the end of the 1990s, they wrapped trees in the park of the **Fondation Beyeler** in Riehen.

Site-specific art is often found in **public spaces**, for example in squares, stations or schools. For many public buildings in Switzerland, part of the money is spent on **art in architecture**. Sometimes there are arguments about whether a work suits its place. If a site-specific work is removed, it is often lost for ever.

gewusst: The “Spiral Jetty” disappeared under water for many years and only reappeared when the water level of the lake fell.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude paid for their huge projects themselves, among other things by selling drawings.

teile.einleitung: Brass is a golden-yellow alloy of copper and zinc. An alloy is a mixture of several metals. Brass is used for musical instruments, door handles, screws and many other things.
wichtigste: Brass consists of **copper and zinc**.
Copper makes up the largest part of it.
Brass shines golden yellow and is easy to work.
Many wind instruments such as trumpets and trombones are made of brass.
Brass is often used for door handles, screws and taps.
Bronze is something different: it consists of copper and tin.

abschnitte.text: Brass is an **alloy**, that is, a mixture of metals. It consists of copper and zinc, with copper making up the larger part. Depending on the mixture, the colour is reddish or pale yellow. More zinc makes brass paler and harder. Brass should not be confused with **bronze**, which consists of copper and tin.

Brass is easy to **cast**, bend, drill and turn. It does not rust like iron. In the air, however, it slowly becomes darker and dull, because a thin layer forms. This layer is called **patina**. With metal polish you can make brass shine again.

Trumpets, trombones, horns and tubas are mostly made of brass. They are called **brass instruments**. Brass can easily be formed into thin tubes and sounds bright and powerful. In many Swiss villages, **music societies** and brass bands play instruments like these. In English such a band is even called a “brass band”, after the metal.

In everyday life you find brass in many places: on **door handles**, locks, keys, screws and taps. Parts in clocks and electrical appliances are also often made of brass. Copper, and therefore brass too, slows down the growth of some germs. That is why it is suitable for handles that many hands touch. Brass is also easy to recycle.

gewusst: The ancient Romans already made brass and minted coins from it.
The English word “brass” is part of the term “brass band”.

teile.einleitung: Simultaneous contrast is a trick of our eyes. A colour looks different depending on the colour around it. Artists use this effect on purpose.
wichtigste: In simultaneous contrast, colours next to each other influence each other.
The eye produces the opposite colour of a colour at the same time.
A grey on red looks slightly greenish.
A grey on black looks lighter than on white.
The Swiss artist Johannes Itten described various colour contrasts.

abschnitte.text: Simultaneous means **at the same time**. When we see a colour, our visual system at the same time produces an impression of its **opposite colour**, the **complementary colour**. This opposite colour slightly tints a neighbouring, neutral area. That is why a grey patch on a red background appears with a hint of **green**. On a green background, however, the same grey looks slightly reddish.

The effect works in a similar way with brightness. A grey patch on a **black** background looks lighter. The same grey on a **white** background looks darker. The grey is exactly the same in both cases. Only the surroundings change our impression.

Painters and designers know about simultaneous contrast and use it deliberately. In this way colours can look brighter or calmer. The Swiss artist **Johannes Itten** taught at the **Bauhaus** and described seven colour contrasts, including simultaneous contrast. His colour theory is still used in schools today.

gewusst: In the 19th century the French chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul studied the effect because dyers were puzzled by seemingly wrong colours in tapestries.

teile.einleitung: Fabrics are with us every day, in clothes, curtains and bed linen. They are made of fibres that are spun into yarn and then woven or knitted.
wichtigste: Cotton comes from the cotton plant.
Linen is made from flax.
Silk comes from the silkworm, wool mostly from sheep.
A sewing pattern helps when cutting out fabric.
The nice outer side of a fabric is called the right side.
Wool can shrink when washed hot.

abschnitte.text: The **cotton plant** forms pods with white, fluffy fibres. **Flax** has long fibres in its stem, from which **linen** is made. The caterpillar of the silk moth spins a long thread for **silk**. **Wool** mostly comes from sheep. There are also synthetic fibres such as **polyester**, which are made from crude oil.

First the fibres are spun into **yarn**. In **weaving**, threads cross at right angles: the warp threads run lengthwise, the weft thread runs across through them. In **knitting**, on the other hand, loops are made that hang into each other. That is why knitted fabrics are stretchier. There is also felt, in which fibres are pressed together without thread.

A **sewing pattern** is a template that shows the shape of the pieces of fabric. You lay it on the fabric, draw round it and cut out the pieces. The nice outer side is called the **right side**, the inner side the **wrong side**. When sewing, you usually put the pieces right sides together. Then you turn the piece the right way out, and the seam is on the inside.

The **care label** tells you how to wash a piece of clothing. If you wash a woollen jumper too hot, the fibres **felt** because of the heat and movement. It **shrinks** and becomes smaller. If a pair of trousers has a hole, you can sew or iron on a **patch**. That way you can keep wearing them, which is good for the environment.

gewusst: The Swiss German word “Leintuch” for a bed sheet comes from the fact that sheets used to be made of linen.
A thread several hundred metres long can be unwound from a single silk cocoon.

teile.einleitung: Romanticism is an era of music that lasted from about 1820 to around 1900. Romantic composers wanted above all to express feelings, dreams, nature and imagination in music. During this time huge orchestral works, famous operas and many songs and piano pieces were written, and they are still among the most popular pieces of classical music today.
wichtigste: Romantic music shaped the period from about 1820 to 1900.
Franz Schubert wrote over 600 songs and shaped the Romantic art song.
Franz Liszt shaped the symphonic poem.
Giuseppe Verdi and Richard Wagner were both born in 1813.
After 1849 Richard Wagner lived in exile in Zurich.
Frédéric Chopin lived in Paris from 1831 until his death in 1849.
The Bayreuth Festival Theatre opened in 1876 with “The Ring of the Nibelung”.

abschnitte.text: Romanticism followed the Viennese Classical period of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. Romantic music often sounds passionate, full of longing or mysterious. Popular themes were nature, love, fairy tales, legends and the night. Many works tell a story without words; this is called **programme music**. Orchestras grew larger, and new tone colours and bold **harmonies** were added.

Franz Schubert from Vienna wrote over 600 songs for voice and piano, for example “Der Erlkönig” (The Erl-King) based on a poem by Goethe. Songs like these are called **art songs**. Robert Schumann and his wife Clara Schumann, a famous pianist, also composed songs and piano pieces. Frédéric Chopin from Poland lived in Paris from 1831 and wrote almost only for the piano, such as waltzes, nocturnes and polonaises. Franz Liszt was the celebrated **virtuoso** of his time.

In 1830 Hector Berlioz wrote the “Symphonie fantastique”, in which a theme representing the beloved keeps coming back: the **idée fixe**. Franz Liszt shaped the **symphonic poem**, an orchestral work in one movement that portrays a poem, a picture or a story. In “Vltava” (The Moldau) Bedřich Smetana described the course of a river; the piece is part of the cycle “Má vlast” (My Homeland). Johannes Brahms, Pyotr Tchaikovsky and Antonín Dvořák also wrote great symphonies.

The two greatest opera composers of Romanticism were born in 1813: Richard Wagner in Leipzig and Giuseppe Verdi in Italy. Verdi wrote operas such as “Aida” and “La Traviata”. Wagner called his works **music dramas** and wrote “The Ring of the Nibelung”, four operas that together last about 15 hours. For these works he had his own festival theatre built in Bayreuth, which opened in 1876. In “Tristan und Isolde” you hear the famous **Tristan chord**, made of the notes F, B, D sharp and G sharp.

After the Dresden May Uprising of 1849 Richard Wagner had to flee and lived in **Zurich** until 1858. Later he lived for some years at Tribschen near Lucerne, where the Richard Wagner Museum stands today. Johannes Brahms spent several summers on **Lake Thun** and composed there. The Swiss Alps thrilled many Romantics, and Liszt wrote piano pieces about places in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A skilfully composed song for voice and piano set to a poem.
An orchestral work that tells a story or depicts a picture with music.
A musician who plays their instrument with extraordinary skill.
A short melody that stands for a character or an idea, typical of Wagner.
Music that describes something outside music, such as a landscape.

gewusst: Franz Liszt was so popular that fans fainted at his concerts; people called it “Lisztomania”.
Franz Schubert lived to be only 31 and still wrote over 600 songs.
To this day the Bayreuth Festival Theatre has a covered orchestra pit, so the audience cannot see the orchestra.

teile.einleitung: The Nouvelle Vague was a movement of young French film-makers at the end of the 1950s. The name means “new wave”. They filmed with little money, on the street and with new ideas, and so changed cinema.
wichtigste: The Nouvelle Vague began in France at the end of the 1950s.
Many of its directors had written film reviews for the magazine “Cahiers du cinéma” before.
In 1960 Jean-Luc Godard made the key film “Breathless”.
Godard was a French-Swiss director and later lived for a long time in Rolle on Lake Geneva.
Typical features are hand-held cameras, real locations and **jump cuts**.
Other important directors were François Truffaut, Claude Chabrol and Agnès Varda.

abschnitte.text: In the 1950s many films in France were made at great expense in the studio. A group of young film lovers found that boring. They wrote reviews for the magazine **“Cahiers du cinéma”** and wanted to do better themselves. At the end of the 1950s they began to make their own films. The press called them the **Nouvelle Vague**, the “new wave”.

The films of the Nouvelle Vague were made with **little money**. Instead of in the studio, they filmed on the street, in cafés and in flats. They often worked with a light **hand-held camera** and natural light. The actors were sometimes allowed to speak freely. Many films told stories about young people and their everyday lives.

In 1960 **Jean-Luc Godard** made the film **“Breathless”**, in French “À bout de souffle”. It became a key film of the movement. Godard used striking jumps in the editing, so-called **jump cuts**. In these, small parts of a scene are missing and the picture jumps. That seemed cheeky and new at the time and is still often copied today.

Jean-Luc Godard was born in Paris in 1930 and also had **Swiss citizenship**. He spent part of his youth in French-speaking Switzerland. Later he lived for many decades in **Rolle on Lake Geneva** and made more films there. He died in Rolle in 2022. Godard is seen as one of the most influential directors in the history of film.

The Nouvelle Vague also included **François Truffaut**, Claude Chabrol, Éric Rohmer and Jacques Rivette. Truffaut’s film “The 400 Blows” from 1959 tells the story of a boy in Paris. The director **Agnès Varda** made films in this new style early on. The ideas of the Nouvelle Vague influenced cinema in many other countries.

gewusst: For “Breathless”, the cameraman sometimes sat in a wheelchair that was pushed along so that he could move smoothly.
Several directors of the Nouvelle Vague were film critics first, before they made films themselves.

teile.einleitung: An orchestra is a large group of musicians who play together on different instruments. It is led by a conductor. A large symphony orchestra can have almost a hundred people and produces a mighty, colourful sound.
wichtigste: An orchestra is led by a conductor.
The conductor often beats time with a baton.
Most of the instruments in the orchestra are string instruments.
The lowest string instrument is the double bass.
For tuning, the oboe usually gives the note A.
The Tonhalle Orchestra Zurich has its home in Zurich.
In many Swiss villages the music society plays mainly wind instruments.

abschnitte.text: An orchestra consists of four large groups. The **string instruments** are the most numerous: violins, violas, cellos and double basses, with the double bass sounding lowest. Then there are the woodwinds, such as the flute, oboe, clarinet and bassoon, and the brass, such as the horn, trumpet, trombone and tuba. The fourth group is the **percussion**, with the large kettledrums (the timpani), cymbals, the triangle and much more.

The musicians sit in a semicircle around the conductor. Right at the front there are usually the **violins**, because they often play the melody. Behind them come the woodwinds, then the brass and right at the back the percussion, because otherwise loud instruments would drown everything out. The first violinist is called the **leader** (concertmaster) and guides the strings.

The person in front of the orchestra is called the **conductor**. With a thin stick, the **baton**, or with their hands, they show the tempo, the entries and the volume. In rehearsals they work out with the orchestra how a piece should sound. To do this they read the score, in which all the parts are written one below the other.

A large orchestra with all the groups of instruments is called a **symphony orchestra**. A smaller one, often with strings only, is called a chamber orchestra. There are also wind orchestras, youth orchestras and opera orchestras. In many Swiss villages the **music society** is an important club in which mainly wind instruments and drums are played, for example at village festivals and on 1 August.

Well-known Swiss orchestras are the **Tonhalle Orchestra Zurich**, the Orchestre de la Suisse Romande in Geneva, the Basel Symphony Orchestra and the Bern Symphony Orchestra. The Orchestre de la Suisse Romande was founded in 1918 by the conductor Ernest Ansermet. Every summer, top orchestras from all over the world also play at the Lucerne Festival in Lucerne. The Swiss Youth Symphony Orchestra gives young talents the chance to play in a large orchestra.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person who leads the orchestra and shows the tempo and entries.
A thin stick with which the conductor beats time.
The first violinist, who leads the strings.
Large kettledrums whose pitch can be adjusted.

gewusst: The oboe gives the tuning note because its sound is clear and piercing and it hardly goes out of tune.
The baton only became common in the 19th century; before that someone often led from the harpsichord or the violin.
Gustav Mahler's 8th Symphony is called the “Symphony of a Thousand” because about a thousand performers took part in the premiere.

teile.einleitung: A readymade is an everyday object that an artist declares to be a work of art, unchanged or hardly changed. The idea was invented by the French artist Marcel Duchamp. His best-known readymade is called “Fountain” and dates from 1917.
wichtigste: A readymade is a ready-made everyday object that is declared to be a work of art.
The idea comes from Marcel Duchamp.
His most famous readymade is “Fountain” from 1917, a signed urinal.
What matters is the idea and the choice, not the craftsmanship.
Readymades had a great influence on 20th-century art.

abschnitte.text: The English word **readymade** means “already made”. Marcel Duchamp took things that a factory had made and exhibited them as art. In 1913 he fixed a bicycle wheel onto a stool; later he showed a bottle rack. He chose the things, sometimes gave them a title and signed them. In this way he asked: what actually makes something art?

In 1917 Duchamp submitted an ordinary **urinal** to an exhibition in New York. He laid it on its back, called it “Fountain” and signed it with the made-up name “R. Mutt”. The organisers did not show it. The original was lost, and today there are only later replicas. Even so, “Fountain” became one of the most famous works of art of the 20th century.

In the past a work of art was thought to be good if it was skilfully painted or carved. Duchamp put the **idea** and the **choice** at the centre. This made many people argue, and it still does today. Later movements such as **conceptual art** or Pop Art built on this thought.

gewusst: Duchamp was a high-level chess player and even played for France at Chess Olympiads.

teile.einleitung: Copyright protects works that people have created, for example pictures, music, texts, films or photos. In Switzerland this is governed by the Copyright Act, URG for short. It decides who may use, copy or publish a work.
wichtigste: A work is protected as soon as it has been created, without registration.
The © sign is only a notice and not a requirement.
Protection lasts until 70 years after the death of the author.
Since 1 April 2020 simple photos without individual character have also been protected.
Photos like this are protected for 50 years from when they were taken.
When protection runs out, a work is in the public domain and may be used freely.

abschnitte.text: **Works** are protected, that is, intellectual creations with an individual character. They include paintings, drawings, songs, books, films, buildings and also computer programs. A mere **idea**, on the other hand, is not protected, only the way it is actually carried out. Whoever creates a work is its **author**. This person decides whether and how their work is used.

In Switzerland you do not have to register or record a work anywhere. Protection arises **automatically** as soon as the work has been created. So even a child’s drawing can be protected. The **©** sign only shows who owns the rights; it is not necessary. The federal office responsible for intellectual property is the Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property in Bern.

A work is protected until **70 years after the death** of the person who created it. After that it is in the **public domain**: everyone may copy, print or adapt it. That is why old paintings and music from the past can often be found freely online. Since the revision of 2020, simple **photos** such as snapshots are also protected. Their protection ends 50 years after the picture was taken.

For **personal use** you may use many things, for example in a private circle with family and friends. Teachers may also use works in lessons. But you may only upload works to the internet or distribute them publicly with permission. Anyone who **quotes** from a work must give the source.
