Organisations such as **SUISA** for music or **ProLitteris** for texts and pictures make sure that authors receive money when their works are used.

gewusst: In Switzerland, protection for computer programs lasts only 50 years after the author’s death.
The works of painters who died more than 70 years ago may be used freely.

teile.einleitung: Plywood is a wood material made of several thin layers of wood. These are glued on top of each other crosswise. This makes a strong board that is often needed in handicraft lessons.
wichtigste: Plywood consists of thin layers of wood glued together.
The fibres of each layer lie across those of the next.
That is why plywood hardly warps.
It usually has an odd number of layers.
Thin plywood is well suited to the fretsaw.

abschnitte.text: Plywood consists of thin layers of wood called **veneers**. They are pressed together with glue. The **wood fibres** of each layer lie across the layer underneath. Plywood usually has an **odd number** of layers, for example three or five. That way the two outer sides run in the same direction.

Solid wood moves: it swells when damp and shrinks when dry, especially across the grain. In the process it can **warp** or crack. In plywood, the layers lying crosswise block each other. That is also where the German name “Sperrholz”, blocking wood, comes from. The board stays flat and is strong in all directions.

Plywood is used for furniture, the backs of cupboards, packaging and models. Thick plywood with many layers is called **multiplex**. In handicraft lessons you cut figures and puzzles out of thin plywood with the **fretsaw**. Then you sand the edges smooth with sandpaper.

gewusst: The veneers for plywood are often peeled off the tree trunk as if from a roll.
Many skateboards are also made of several layers of wood glued together.

teile.einleitung: For centuries the textile industry was one of the most important branches of the Swiss economy. Linen, silk, fabric printing and embroidery made whole regions famous.
wichtigste: St Gallen became rich from linen made of flax as early as the late Middle Ages.
In the 19th century Zurich was an important silk city.
Glarus was famous for fabric printing, the Glarus cloth printing.
Eastern Switzerland later became known for embroidery.
Rieter from Winterthur builds spinning machines for the whole world.
In the past many people worked at home and in factories.

abschnitte.text: As early as the **late Middle Ages**, St Gallen was an important trading place for **linen**. It was made from **flax** and strictly inspected in the city. Only good goods received a quality mark. St Gallen linen was sold all over Europe. This tradition later formed the basis for the famous **embroidery**.

In the 19th century **Zurich** was a centre of **silk weaving** and the silk trade. Many families on Lake Zurich wove at home on looms. Merchants bought the fabrics and sold them abroad. The **Seidengasse**, Silk Lane, in Zurich is still a reminder of this today.

In the 19th century the canton of **Glarus** was famous for **fabric printing**. In large print works, cotton fabrics were printed with colourful patterns. Many cloths were exported, including to Asia and Africa. People speak of **Glarus cloth printing**.

In the 19th century many **spinning mills** and weaving mills were built on rivers, because the water drove the machines. Children and adults often worked very long hours. The federal **Factory Act** of 1877 limited working hours and banned factory work for young children. **Mechanical engineering** also grew out of the textile industry: the company **Rieter** in Winterthur, founded in the 18th century, is today one of the largest makers of spinning machines.

gewusst: Many Swiss engineering companies have their roots in the textile industry.
Around 1910 embroidery was Switzerland’s largest export industry.

teile.einleitung: Materials testing examines how strong, hard or tough a material is. This tells you whether a bridge, a bike frame or a fabric can take the load. A distinction is made between tests that destroy the sample and tests that leave it undamaged.
wichtigste: Empa is the Swiss research institute for materials science.
Mechanical stress is force divided by cross-sectional area.
The tensile test produces the stress-strain diagram.
In the Vickers method, a diamond pyramid is pressed into the material.
On the Mohs scale, diamond has the highest value, 10.
The Charpy impact test shows toughness.
Ultrasonic testing is a form of non-destructive testing.

abschnitte.text: **Empa** is the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology. It has sites in Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun and belongs to the **ETH Domain**. Its roots go back to 1880, when an institute for testing building materials was founded in Zurich. Today Empa tests and researches materials for building, energy, medicine and much more. It works closely with universities and companies.

In the **tensile test**, a test bar is clamped and slowly pulled apart until it breaks. During this, the force and the lengthening are measured. **Stress** is calculated as force divided by area: 10,000 newtons on 20 mm² gives 500 N/mm², that is, 500 megapascals. In the **stress-strain diagram** you can see the **yield point**, the **tensile strength** and the modulus of elasticity. This tells you from what point a material is permanently deformed.

Hardness means how strongly a material resists another body pushing into it. In the **Vickers method**, a four-sided **diamond pyramid** is pressed into the sample and the diagonal of the dent is measured. **Brinell**, on the other hand, uses a ball. For minerals there is the **Mohs scale** from 1 to 10. It orders minerals by which can scratch which: talc has 1, diamond 10.

In the **Charpy impact test**, a heavy pendulum hammer breaks through a notched sample. The energy used shows whether a material is **tough** or breaks in a **brittle** way. This is important for steel, which must not suddenly break even in the cold. For textiles, resistance to rubbing is tested with the **Martindale test**. In it, a test head rubs over the fabric in circular movements until damage can be seen.

In **non-destructive testing**, the part stays whole. In **ultrasonic testing**, sound waves are sent into it and the echoes that form at cracks are analysed. With **X-rays** you can look inside welded seams. In this way, for example, aircraft parts, railway wheels and pipelines are checked. Faults are found before anything dangerous happens.

gewusst: One newton per square millimetre is exactly one megapascal.
The Mohs scale was developed by the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs.

teile.einleitung: Upcycling means making something new and more valuable out of waste or old things. An object is redesigned without its material first being broken down. This is kind to the environment and is often fun too.
wichtigste: In upcycling, something old is turned into something more valuable.
The material is not melted down or broken down, but used again directly.
One example is a bag made from an old pair of jeans.
Upcycling saves raw materials, energy and waste.
Recycling, on the other hand, breaks material down and turns it into new raw material.
In downcycling, something of lower value is produced.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from English: “up” means upwards and “cycling” refers to a cycle. In **upcycling**, an old object gets a second life. It is cut, sewn, painted or put together in a new way. In the end it is more useful or more beautiful than before. The term became known in the 1990s.

In **recycling**, material is collected and processed, for example PET bottles, glass or paper. This produces new raw material, but it needs energy. In **upcycling**, the object stays almost as it is and is only redesigned. In **downcycling**, a material is turned into something of lower value, for example paper into low-grade cardboard. All three ways are better than simply throwing things away.

You can easily try out upcycling at home or in handicraft lessons. An old pair of **jeans** becomes a bag, a T-shirt a shopping bag. Tins become pencil holders, old jars become lanterns. You can build furniture out of wooden pallets. The important thing is to be careful with sharp tools.

A well-known Swiss example is the bags made by the company **Freitag** from Zurich. In 1993 the brothers Markus and Daniel Freitag began sewing bags from used lorry tarpaulins. They also use old bicycle inner tubes and seat belts. Every bag looks different, because every tarpaulin has different colours and marks. Today these bags are known in many countries.

gewusst: With Freitag bags, no tarpaulin is cut up in the same way twice, which is why every bag is one of a kind.
Artists also make works of art out of rubbish; this is often called trash art.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Hirschhorn is a Swiss artist who mainly builds large installations. For them he uses cheap everyday materials such as cardboard, sticky tape and kitchen foil. His works are meant to make people think and join in.
wichtigste: Thomas Hirschhorn was born in Bern in 1957.
He has lived and worked in Paris since the 1980s.
Typical materials are cardboard, sticky tape, kitchen foil, plastic sheeting and photocopies.
His installations are often walk-in, so you can go inside them.
In 2011 he represented Switzerland at the Venice Biennale.

abschnitte.text: Hirschhorn deliberately builds his works out of things that everyone knows and that cost little. **Cardboard**, **sticky tape** and **kitchen foil** look simple and sometimes even unfinished. With them he wants to show that art does not have to be expensive and shiny. Everyone should feel welcome in front of his works. Newspaper cuttings, books and pictures are often stuck on the walls too.

His **monuments** to philosophers are well known. They are not memorials of stone, but simple buildings of wood and cardboard that only stand for a short time. They are often built in residential areas where little art can usually be seen. A well-known example is the “Gramsci Monument” from 2013 in New York. People from the neighbourhood helped build it and used the place for readings, courses and meetings.

abschnitte.titel: A Swiss man in the world
abschnitte.text: Hirschhorn studied design in Zurich and then moved to France. He has exhibited in many large museums and at **documenta** in Kassel. At the **Venice Biennale** in 2011 he designed the Swiss pavilion with a huge installation. His art is often political and sparks discussions. Some find it important and brave, others rather uncomfortable.

gewusst: In 2000 Hirschhorn received the Prix Marcel Duchamp, an important French art prize.
Many of his works only stand for a few weeks and are then taken down again.

teile.einleitung: A vice is a clamping tool that sits on the workbench in almost every workshop. It holds a workpiece firmly so that you can saw, file or drill it safely.
wichtigste: A vice holds workpieces firmly between two jaws.
One jaw is fixed, the other is moved by a spindle.
You turn the handle, and the spindle pushes the jaws together.
The vice is screwed firmly to the workbench.
Soft jaws made of aluminium, plastic or wood prevent marks.

abschnitte.text: A vice has two **jaws** between which you put the workpiece. One jaw is fixed to the body, the other can be moved. It is moved by a **spindle**, a long screw with a thread. When you turn the handle, the movable jaw moves forwards or backwards. This creates a strong clamping force, even though you only need a little strength.

The jaws of a metal vice are usually **grooved** so that the workpiece does not slip. But these grooves press into soft materials such as wood, copper or painted parts. That is why you put **soft jaws** in between. They are made of aluminium, plastic or wood and protect the surface. Some soft jaws are held on the vice by magnets.

A workpiece that is well clamped cannot slip away while you work. So you have both hands free for the saw or file. You clamp the workpiece as close to the jaws as possible so that it does not vibrate when you saw. You only tighten the handle by hand and never lengthen it with a pipe, otherwise the vice can break. For woodwork there are also workbenches with built-in **wooden vices**.

gewusst: Large vices can clamp so tightly that soft metal gets bent out of shape in them.
There are also machine vices that you place on the table of a pillar drill.
